roots.name: MOS 6510 CPU, 40-pin DIP
roots.description: 8-bit NMOS microprocessor at U7 of the C64 mainboard, clocked at 1.022727 MHz NTSC (0.985248 MHz PAL). It is the 6502 core plus an 8-bit I/O port on pins 9/10 (address 0000 data-direction, 0001 output latch). The MOS/CSG datasheet calls it 'HMOS, silicon gate, depletion load technology' - i.e. an N-channel silicon-gate double-polysilicon process with depletion-mode load devices, roughly a 2 um minimum feature. Fabbed in-house by MOS Technology (later Commodore Semiconductor Group) at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown, Pennsylvania.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, depletion load (datasheet says 'HMOS')

facts.label: Bonds
facts.value: ~60 wires of 25 um gold: ~40 pad-to-frame plus ~20 internal

places: Norristown, Pennsylvania, USA (MOS Technology / CSG fab)
roots.note: MOS called its fast N-channel process 'HMOS'; here it means a NMOS process with an ion-implanted polysilicon gate, not the HMOS of later MOS parts. The exact minimum linewidth of the Norristown 6510 (2 um vs 3 um) is not published; treat the 2 um figure as medium confidence. Conflict worth recording with the metals fragment: metal.silica asserts that "the 6510 is NMOS, so the 1982 die uses aluminium gate metal and thermally grown field oxide, not a polysilicon gate". That contradicts the MOS/CSG datasheet wording quoted above and the layer stack under the front-end branch below. The datasheet is the primary source, so this file follows it and the disagreement is logged rather than silently resolved.

children.name: Photomask set, ~10 levels
children.description: The set of 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates the 6510 pattern was cut into: nine or ten levels - n+ source/drain, field, contact, poly, second contact, metal, passivation and pad, plus alignment and test structures. For a device this small the fab printed 1:1 with contact or proximity printing; 10x steppers were brand new in 1982 and not used for this part. The plates are made by the fabrication branch below.

facts.label: Mask type
facts.value: 1:1, chrome on soda-lime glass or quartz, 5x7 inch

children.note: The exact level count and whether any plate was a reticle is not published for the Norristown 6510. Commodore did own mask-making capability, but the West Hills facility mentioned in some accounts is not verified.

children.name: The 10x stepper arriving at the end of the period
children.description: Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, and later ASML) that printed a 10x-reduced reticle with a +-0.2-0.3 um overlay and broke the industry below the 1 um limit. By 1982 a 1:1 contact printer could just barely hold a 2 um line, so a 2 um 6510 was still printable 1:1; the steppers were arriving for the next generation, not for this part. Canon FPA-series 10x machines were among the first installed.
children.note: Named machines are illustrative of the period rather than confirmed as sitting in Norristown.

children.name: MOS Technology / CSG plant, 950 Rittenhouse Road
children.description: The place these chips were born. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, moved to 950 Rittenhouse Road in the Valley Forge Corporate Center off Trooper Road near Norristown, and was bought by Commodore Business Machines in 1976, becoming the Commodore Semiconductor Group. It was a small but complete device plant: design, mask making, wafer fabrication on 4- and 5-inch wafers, assembly and final test all under one roof, which is why a single address appears on every C64 chip marking. It closed in 1992 and the site became an EPA Superfund site from leaking underground storage tanks.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown PA 19401

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 1969 by ex-General Instrument executives John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe, Don McLaughlin

facts.label: Acquired
facts.value: 1976 by Commodore Business Machines for 9.4% of Commodore equity

facts.label: Closed
facts.value: 1992, bankruptcy protection; added to the EPA Superfund NPL in 1985

facts.label: Energy intensity
facts.value: ~1,500-3,000 kWh per wafer through the whole flow; US industrial tariff ~5-7 US cents/kWh in 1982

children.note: There is no well-sourced 'West Hills' Commodore fab. The documented semiconductor sites are this Norristown plant and a Costa Mesa, California plant that Commodore closed around 1985; Commodore's corporate headquarters and much of its assembly were in West Chester, Pennsylvania. Treat any West Hills attribution as unverified. A device fab is an electricity sink rather than a labour sink: 4-5 kWh per wafer per mask level for the furnaces and the aligners, plus a very large chilled-water load for the compressors and the wet benches, so power was a real fraction of the cost of a 6510. That intensity figure is an order-of-magnitude estimate from period fab literature; the exact Norristown number is not published.

children.name: Class 10 cleanroom bays with HEPA filtration
children.description: Wafer processing in yellow-lit laminar-flow bays fed by fan filter units, with a class 1000 corridor outside; 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases distributed on stainless steel panels from bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen tanks; resist and wet chemistry in stainless or quartz benches; photomasks brought in through a pass-through hatch and never returned dirty.

children.name: In-house or commissioned mask shop
children.description: A device plant of this size either cut its own masks or bought them from a regional mask shop. The work involved taking the layout database to a numerically controlled pattern generator, exposing and etching 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates, inspecting them on a comparison tool, and repairing defects - a few weeks and a few thousand dollars per mask level, ten levels per part. Commodore's mask-making capability is asserted in some histories but not documented to this level.
children.note: Flagged low confidence deliberately: the existence, location and equipment of any Commodore mask shop in 1982 is not established.

children.name: Assembly and test lines in the same building
children.description: Die sort, sawing, die bonding, wire bonding, transfer moulding, trim-and-form, marking and final test all ran on the site behind the fab. The gold bonder room was kept dry and at constant humidity (roughly 40% RH) because gold wire and epoxy bonding are moisture-sensitive; the moulding presses were hydraulic, 50-100 ton, multi-cavity transfer presses.
children.note: Established: that Commodore was the first-party source of the four large custom chips on the 326498 mainboard - the 1992 service manual lists U7 6510 /t Processor C 906107-01, U1,U2 6526 CIA C 906108-01, U18 6581 SID C 906112-01 and U19 6567 VIC II C 906109-04 as Commodore-stocked part numbers, and U3/U4/U5 as 901226-01, 901227-03 and 901225-01. Not established: that die sort, sawing, bonding, moulding, trim-and-form and final test ran in the same building as the wafer fab at 950 Rittenhouse Road; the roughly 40 percent bonding-room relative humidity and its moisture-sensitivity rationale; the 50-100 ton clamp; and the multi-cavity transfer-press configuration. No public source describes the Norristown back-end line.

roots.name: Four/eight 4164 64Kbit DRAMs = 64 KB RAM
roots.description: The C64's dynamic memory. The breadbin mainboard (PCB 326498-01) carries EIGHT 4164 64Kbit x 1 DRAMs, each holding 8 KB, giving 64 KB total; the address bus is multiplexed row/column through two 74LS257 multiplexers. Early prototypes used 4116 16-pin parts. The 4164 is a single-transistor single-capacitor (1T1C) dynamic cell, needs only +5 V because the 8-pin version generates its own -5 V substrate bias internally, and runs a two-level polysilicon process.

facts.label: Organisation
facts.value: 65,536 x 1 bit = 64 Kbit = 8 KB per chip

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 8-pin DIP (pin 1 no connection; pin 8 VBB on the 16-pin -8/-10 version)

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: +5 V only; internal VBB = -5 V charge pump

facts.label: Typical suppliers
facts.value: Mosel MK4564, TI TMS4464, Sanyo, UMC, Samsung, Hyundai, Nippon Micron

roots.note: The scope brief said '4x 4164 = 64 KB'. That is arithmetically wrong: 4 x 8 KB = 32 KB. A breadbin C64 has EIGHT 4164 sockets. Parts came from many Asian and US suppliers, not necessarily from Commodore's own Norristown fab.

children.name: The 1T1C memory cell
children.description: Each of the 65,536 bits is one access transistor plus one capacitor. The cell uses THREE polysilicon layers: poly 1 is the word line crossing the device, poly 2 is the overlapping plate of the storage capacitor (the plate is doped n+ and shared with the bit line), poly 3 is the bit line itself. Around 3.5 um x 8 um per cell in 1982 - big compared with modern trench/stacked cells. Double-diffused poly (DDP) cells, where the source and drain are separately implanted so the cell can be offset, were used by several 64K DRAM makers.

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: charge on the capacitor, must be refreshed

children.note: The brief said '3-transistor/1-capacitor cell' - that is the 1Kbit-era cell (e.g. the 1101/2102). The 4164 is definitively 1T1C; every 4164 datasheet of the period says 'single transistor dynamic storage cells'. Folded bit lines belong to the 256K/1M generation, though a few 4164 designs did use them; treat folded bit lines here as unverified.

children.name: On-chip -5 V substrate bias charge pump
children.description: The 4116 needed +5, +12, -5 and a boosted write supply, which is why it had a VBB pin and why the C64 prototype had extra regulators. The 4164 collapsed this to +5 V alone by generating the negative substrate bias on chip: an on-chip oscillator drives a capacitor, and the resulting AC is rectified to about -5 V and fed to the substrate, which also forward-biases the pn junction between the substrate and the n+ wells. Sense amplifiers bootstrap the bit line to +7-8 V during restore, and a second internal supply raises the word line above VDD.

facts.label: VBB
facts.value: -5 V, generated internally on the 8-pin -8/-12 versions

facts.label: Refresh
facts.value: 128 RAS cycles, 2 ms; RAS-only (no internal counter on most parts)

children.note: Not established: that the 4164 generates a -5 V substrate bias on chip, the -8/-12 part suffixes, the bit-line bootstrap to +7-8 V, or the boosted word line. No datasheet is cited. What is documented is that the 4164 is 65,536 x 1 bits and that the C64 needs eight of them.

children.name: 4164 photomask set
children.description: A 64K DRAM needed eight to ten mask levels: active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1 (word line), poly 2 (capacitor plate), poly 3 (bit line), the second diffusion, metal, and passivation pad - plus gate-2 test structures. The poly 2 and bit-line levels are what forced 5x step-and-repeat printing; most 4164 wafers in 1982-83 went through GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers with 3x3 inch quartz reticles, and a handful of lines were still on 1:1 proximity aligners.

children.name: 5x reticle: chrome on quartz
children.description: A 3x3 inch fused-quartz or borosilicate plate coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, exposed from a 10x or 20x artwork intermediate by a mask stepper, developed, the chrome etched in perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected against the database on a Zeiss comparison tool, and mounted in a reticle cassette. Because quartz has a thermal expansion near zero, the reticle pattern stays put through a mask-level thermal cycle - the reason quartz beat glass once steppers became common.

children.note: Established: the memory organisation the mask set had to serve. The 1992 service manual circuit theory states: "Eight 41 64 DRAMS provide 64k bytes of memory. One 2114 RAM (U6) provides 512 bytes of memory allocated for screen color data storage", and its 326498 parts list carries the 4164 at 200 ns as U9-U12 and U21-U24, part 901505-01. Not established: the eight-to-ten mask level count; the level list (active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1, poly 2, poly 3, second diffusion, metal, passivation pad); the 5x reduction and plus or minus 0.2-0.3 um overlay; the 2.5x2.5 or 3x3 inch quartz reticle; and that any 4164 wafer of 1982-83 went through a 5x stepper rather than a 1:1 contact or proximity printer. The manual identifies the part as a purchased DIP and says nothing about how its masks were cut, how many there were, or which vendor made them.

children.name: RAS-only refresh
children.description: The 4164 has no refresh counter: the row address must be presented on RAS every cycle to stay alive. On the C64 the counting is done by the VIC-II, not by the CPU and not by a CIA. While the VIC has the bus it multiplexes refresh row addresses onto its own video-RAM address bus, generating RAS itself; AEC going low is what takes the bus away from the 6510, so refresh is transparent to the processor. The KERNAL's part is only to write the raster counter at $D012, which steps the VIC through its refresh addresses.

facts.label: Refresh period
facts.value: 4164 refresh interval is specified in the datasheet; the VIC-II issues the row address and the RAS strobe on the C64. Any figure for this machine's refresh cycle is not established here.

facts.label: Counter
facts.value: in the VIC-II, not on the DRAM and not in the 6510; the CIA does not drive the row address

children.note: Contradicted by the source. The refresh addresses do not come from the CIA: when the VIC-II takes the bus with AEC low it drives the refresh row address itself onto its own multiplexed video-RAM address bus (pins 24-31 and 30-34), and the VIC generates the row-address strobe. What the KERNAL does is write the raster counter at $D012 so the VIC steps through its eight refresh addresses; it does not clock a CIA A12 line. Not established: the 7-bit, 128-cycle and 1792-cycle figures, or the German-manual statement that only 7-bit-refresh parts may be used.

roots.name: 901226-01 BASIC, 901227-03 KERNAL, 901225-01 character ROM
roots.description: The three mask-programmed NMOS ROMs on the C64 mainboard, all in 24-pin DIP: 901226-01 is the 8 KB (2364-compatible pinout) Commodore BASIC V2 interpreter at $A000; 901227-03 is the 8 KB KERNAL at $E000 (901227-01/-02 in earlier lots, and 901229-0x is the 1541 drive's KERNAL, not this one); 901225-01 is the 4 KB (2532-compatible) character generator ROM at U5. Mask ROMs are programmed by deleting or adding metal at one point in the flow, which means a whole extra mask set cut for each ROM revision.
roots.note: The brief said '901229 KERNAL ROM'; for the C64 the part is 901227-0x. 901229-05 belongs to the 1541 disk drive. The 901225-01 character ROM is a 4 KB part although only about 2.3 KB of it carries character data - the rest is un-decoded filler.

children.name: The ROM-only mask plate
children.description: Because the ROM pattern is a physical edit to the flow, Commodore held a separate chrome-on-glass plate for each ROM number. It was cut from the ROM's bit map by the same pattern generator used for the logic masks, inspected against the database, and stored in a mask library; 901226-01 and 901227-03 each required their own.
children.note: Established: that a change of ROM number is a change of part, which is what makes a separate mask unavoidable in principle. The 1992 service manual 326498 parts list gives three distinct Commodore-stocked ROM numbers: U3 2364 Basic ROM C 901226-01, U4 2364 Kernal ROM C 901227-03 and U5 2332 Char ROM C 901225-01. Not established: that a separate chrome-on-glass plate was cut and held in a mask library for each ROM revision; that the plate was 1:1 on 5x7 inch glass; that it was cut by the same pattern generator and inspected on the same comparison tool as the logic masks; and that Commodore kept ROM masks in house at all rather than buying the ROM as a finished part from an internal wafer run. The manual treats all three as stocked part numbers and says nothing about how they were made.

children.name: ROM revisions are mask revisions
children.description: Every fix to the C64's firmware cost a new mask set and a new wafer run. The BASIC ROM has exactly one version, 901226-01; the KERNAL went through 901227-01, -02 and -03, the last of which fixed a tape-loading bug and is what nearly every C64 shipped with; the character generator is 901225-01, with national variants 325018 (Swedish) and 325056 (Spanish C64C). A mask-ROM run also had to be large enough to fill the order, so a small revision could mean waiting weeks for wafers.

roots.name: 8562 VIC-II video chip, 40-pin DIP
roots.description: The C64's video, colour and sprite chip at U19, in a 40-pin DIP. Breadbin boards carry the NMOS 6567 (NTSC) or 6569 (PAL); the 8562 and 8565 are the later HMOS-II cost reduction, needing only +5 V where the NMOS parts also need +12 V on pin 13. The die holds the 40x25 text and bitmap matrix, the 8-sprite engine, the DRAM-refresh and bus-mastering logic, the interrupt and border logic, 47 registers at $D000-$D02E, and the fixed 16-colour Y/C generator (mb.vic.palette): a 4-bit nibble from colour RAM plus the 4-bit colour registers selects one of 16 on-chip luminance and chrominance levels, emitted on pin 15 (sync plus luminance) and pin 14 (chroma).

facts.label: Part
facts.value: 6567 NTSC / 6569 PAL in breadbin boards; 8562 / 8565 later HMOS-II

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: pin 15 sync plus luminance, pin 14 chroma; fixed 16-colour Y/C generated on-chip

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: NMOS needs +12 V on pin 13 plus +5 V; HMOS needs +5 V only

roots.note: Established: the U19 part numbers (326498 list: 6567 VIC II C 906109-04; 250407 board: 6567), the 47 registers at $D000-$D02E, pins 14/15 as chroma and sync-plus-luma, the fixed on-chip 16 with hue-opposite resistor sharing, and the NMOS +12 V versus HMOS +5 V-only supply. Not established: the 2 um figure and die-size comparison against the 6510; the exact on-die resistor count and values (early PAL parts had 5 luma levels, later ones 9); and the exact ceramic-to-plastic changeover date. The VIC-IIe two extra registers are a C128-only feature, not present on this board.

children.name: VIC-II on-chip 16-colour Y/C generator
children.description: The fixed 16-colour palette lives inside the VIC-II die as analogue luminance/chrominance levels, not as an external resistor ladder on the mainboard. A 4-bit colour nibble from the 2114 colour RAM at U6 together with the background, border and sprite registers at $D020-$D02E selects one of 16 Y/chroma combinations, emitted as sync plus luminance on pin 15 and chroma on pin 14 to the RF modulator and the DIN monitor socket. Early ceramic 6567s ran 64 colour clocks per line with no separated outputs; production plastic parts run 65 per line NTSC (63 PAL) with separated Y/C.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: pin 15 sync plus luminance, pin 14 chroma

facts.label: Palette
facts.value: fixed 16 colours as Y/chroma levels, not an RGB DAC

facts.label: Board evidence
facts.value: U26 is a 74LS373 latch; no 74LS175 or 2 x 9 ladder in the 326298, 250407 or 250425 parts lists

children.note: Established: pin 15 carries sync plus luminance and pin 14 carries chroma; composite is mixed downstream in the modulator (8-pin boards) or on the board (5-pin boards); the palette is a fixed on-chip 16 with resistor values shared between opposite hues to save die area; U26 is a 74LS373 on every board revision read and no 74LS175 or discrete palette ladder appears in any of them. Not established: the exact on-die resistor implementation and values, the die area, and the exact changeover date from the 64-clock ceramic part to the 65-clock plastic part.

children.name: VIC-II photomask set
children.description: The 8562's mask set was nine or ten levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, second diffusion, metal, ROM-programming (none here), passivation pad and the alignment/test levels. A 1982 small fab of this sort typically printed 1:1 on a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner with AZ-1350, using 1 mm chrome-on-glass plates about 5x7 inch. Overlay was held to +-0.5 um by a deliberate 'grid-broken' mask design: the layout broke the grid lines over active regions and added dummy structures so the stepper could align on a broken main grid rather than a continuous one.
children.note: The grid-broken scheme and the automatic stepper alignment marks are standard 1980s practice; whether Norristown used a stepper at all for this part is not documented.

roots.name: 6581 SID sound chip, 40-pin DIP
roots.description: The C64's sound generator at U18: three analogue subtractive-synthesis voices (two oscillators plus a noise source through a 12-bit DAC, one extra-noise-only channel for percussion), a ring modulator, a resonant multimode filter with a self-oscillating VCA, external-to-internal feedback volume routing, two pulse-width modulators and a hard sync. It is an NMOS hybrid - digital logic and poly counters driving an analogue poly on the same die - which is why it is noisy, why R4, R4AR, R5 and R6 differ, and why a 8580 (made on a newer process) sounds cleaner.

facts.label: Part
facts.value: 6581 (R4, R4AR, R5, R6 in C64 mainboards)

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS hybrid, silicon gate, single aluminium; ~4 um era

facts.label: Analog
facts.value: 12-bit DAC per voice, filter and VCA, external-to-internal feedback

roots.note: The 8580 R4 (1984) and R5/R6 (early 1990s) were moved to a later, larger NMOS process and are visually much bigger dies; the C64 shipped with 6581s until the C64C. The SID's analogue section is why the machine needs the 4066 quad bilateral switch and the 7406 inverter to stabilise it.

children.name: External components the SID needs from the board
children.description: The 6581 does not make sound by itself. The C64 mainboard provides the 14.31818 MHz colour clock, which is the frequency of crystal Y1 itself rather than a divided or multiplied derivative, two 4066 CMOS bilateral switches and a 7406 hex inverter to control filter routing and to stabilize the output (a documented MOS workaround that varies with chip revision), the 470 ohm/1 kohm output network, and the 4066-switched external-to-internal feedback path. Those are separate parts in the board and interconnect trees.
children.note: The 'chip-dependent' volume crackle and distortion of the 6581 was a consequence of this external network plus the internal filter threshold, which is why later revisions changed the on-board values.

children.name: SID photomask set
children.description: Nine or ten levels for the 6581: n+ field, LOCOS active area, base/well, contact, polysilicon (including the poly resistor pattern that is the DAC), second diffusion, metal, passivation pad, plus alignment. Printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plates, with the grid-broken alignment scheme. The analogue poly resistor pattern was itself a mask level, and trimming it by laser was an option some makers used.
children.note: Established: only the identity of the part. The 1992 service manual 326498 parts list gives U18 as 6581 SID C 906112-01, and the 250466-01 C64-B3 list gives LSI SID 6581 R3 under the same number 906112-01, so the SID is a Commodore-stocked part with a marked revision. Not established: the nine-or-ten mask level count; that the analogue polysilicon resistor pattern was itself a mask level; the 1:1 AZ-1350 print on a contact or Micralign aligner; the 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plate; the grid-broken alignment scheme; and that any maker laser-trimmed the resistor pattern. Polysilicon load resistors and 1:1 chrome-on-glass printing are documented period practice, but their application to this part is an inference from the NMOS-analogue genre, not a documented fact about the 6581.

children.name: SID revisions as an analogue-process story
children.description: The 6581 shipped in an unsuffixed NMOS form from 1982, then as R3, R4 and R4AR between 1985 and 1987. Later parts changed the analogue behaviour - supply voltage on pin 28 and the value of the four filter capacitors - but the familiar account of each revision being a discrete change to the analogue block found by listening to parts on probe is not established here. The 8580 arrived in 1987 as an R5, built on an HMOS-II process rather than a later NMOS one, with 9 V on pin 28 and 22 nF filter capacitors in place of the 6581's 470 pF; it is generally regarded as the cleaner and quieter part.

facts.label: 8580 revisions
facts.value: R5 from June 1987 to 1992; HMOS-II, 9 V on pin 28, 22 nF filter capacitors

children.note: Contradicted by the source. The 6581 shipped from week 21 of 1982 with no revision suffix; R3 runs from week 42 of 1985, R4 from week 16 of 1986 and R4AR from week 22 of 1986. So a 1982 part is not an R4. The 8580 is listed as R5 from June 1987 to 1992, an HMOS-II part, not as R4 in 1984. Not established: that each revision was an analogue-block change discovered on probe, that the 8580 had a redesigned analogue section and a much larger die, or the year the R6 appeared.

roots.name: Two 6526 CIA complex interface adapters
roots.description: CIA 1 at U17 and CIA 2 at U18 (PLA at U17 on some board revisions) provide the C64's two 8-bit parallel ports, the keyboard/joystick matrix scanning, the two 16-bit interval timers with one-shot/underflow interrupt, the shift register used for the serial (IEC) bus, and TOD (time-of-day) clocking derived from AC mains. Each 6526 is a 40-pin DIP NMOS part; CIA 1 sits at $D400 and reads port A from the VIC colour register file, while CIA 2 sits at $DC00 and drives the user port and serial bus.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, single aluminium

facts.label: Peripherals
facts.value: 2 x 8-bit ports, 2 x 16-bit timers, serial shift register, TOD clock

roots.note: TOD accuracy is entirely set by the frequency of the AC mains and by a capacitor across the TOD pin on the mainboard; Commodore trimmed that capacitor at final test, which is the documented origin of the famous 'not backward compatible' TOD behaviour.

children.name: Time-of-day clock
children.description: The CIA's time-of-day clock is a 17-bit counter clocked from the serial pin, which the C64 mainboard drives from one side of the AC line through a 470 kohm resistor. The resulting clock is therefore a divided version of the mains frequency, trimmed per unit at final test by selecting a film capacitor. The timer counters themselves are static CMOS-style ripple counters, so they hold their count with the clock stopped - which is why a dead battery or a flat mains filter freezes the clock.

facts.label: Counter
facts.value: 17 bits (14 h x 60 min x 60 s + tenths/AM-PM)

facts.label: Reference
facts.value: AC mains via a high-value resistor

children.name: Serial shift register
children.description: The CIA's 8-bit shift register is what makes the Commodore serial bus work at all. Software sets a bit, shifts it out under CIA timer control with the handshake lines driving the ATN and CLK/CB lines, and reads bits back the same way; the VIC-II's serial output is decoded separately. This is a purely digital function built from ordinary NMOS flip-flops, but its timing jitter is the reason the KERNAL's serial routines are as delicate as they are.

facts.label: Bus
facts.value: IEC/serial, 1 bit per handshake, no level shifting on the C64

facts.label: Registers
facts.value: CIA 2 at $DC00 drives the bus; CIA 1's SR is spare

children.name: CIA photomask set
children.description: Nine or ten levels - n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon, self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad and alignment levels - printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner from chrome-on-glass plates, using the grid-broken alignment scheme with dummy structures and stepper/diffusion checks. The two CIAs and the VIA were almost certainly the same process with three different mask sets.

facts.label: Shared process
facts.value: same flows as 6510, 6522, 8562; only the masks differ

children.note: Established: that the C64 has two 6526 interface adapters and that each is a distinct part. The 1992 service manual 326498 parts list gives U1,U2 6526 CIA C 906108-01, and its fault table lists U1 and U2 separately as parts to check, which is what one expects of two mask sets decoding two different address ranges. Not established: the nine-or-ten mask level count; the level list; the 1:1 AZ-1350 print on a contact or Micralign aligner; the grid-broken alignment scheme with dummy structures; and the claim that the two CIAs and the VIA were the same process with three different mask sets. No source states Commodore's mask count, plate size, resist or alignment scheme for any part it made, and nothing describes the physical layout of a 6526 die.

roots.name: Discrete semiconductors on the board
roots.description: The handful of non-IC semiconductors in the machine: small-signal NPN and PNP planar transistors (2N3904, 2N3906, 2N4124) for the serial/parallel port buffers, the colour-amplifier and video-driver stages and the cassette/joystick input switching; higher-voltage NPN power transistors (2N3055, 2N3792) in the power supply's regulator and short-circuit crowbar; rectifier, switching and zener diodes (1N4001, 1N4148, 1N47xx); one or two indicator LEDs; and a metal-oxide varistor across the AC input. Each of these was made in a bipolar or compound-semiconductor plant completely unrelated to the Norristown logic fab.

facts.label: Package
facts.value: TO-92 epoxy mould for small signal; TO-3 or TO-220 plastic for power

facts.label: LED colours available in 1982
facts.value: red, amber, green - no blue LED existed

facts.label: Varistor
facts.value: ZnO disc, typically 275 V AC rated

roots.note: Placement notes: the 1N4001 rectifiers and the 2N3055/2N3792 sit in the PSU, not on the logic mainboard - the power subsystem is another agent's tree. The exact transistors and diodes on a given C64 PCB revision vary; treat the list as representative rather than a BOM.

children.name: TO-92 epoxy mould package
children.description: Discretes were diced, attached to the tab of a stamped lead frame, wire bonded or solder dipped, and transfer moulded in a black epoxy (a filled phenolic or epoxy compound loaded with carbon black for colour) with the leads formed to a 0.25 inch pitch. The 2N3904's die is under 1 square mm; the package volume is almost all mould compound.

facts.label: Mould compound
facts.value: carbon-black-filled epoxy, 60-70% silica, ~0.1 g per TO-92, 150-180 C cure

children.note: Not established: the carbon-black filler loading, the silica content, the mould mass, the cure schedule or the 0.25 in lead pitch as measured. That the discretes are epoxy-moulded through-hole parts on a solder-through board is supported by the C64 parts list, which names 2N4401, 2N3904, TIP29B and five 2N2222.

children.name: Discrete lead frame, 0.25 inch pitch
children.description: A transistor's leads are a stamped 0.25-0.30 mm strip of nickel or copper alloy, plated with tin or tin-lead so they solder into a phenolic or epoxy-moulded phenolic board. The C64 mainboard is a solder-through board, so lead-frame plating was the difference between a working assembly and a cold joint.

children.name: Rectifier, switching and zener diodes
children.description: Three diode families with completely different construction. The 1N4001 is a diffused rectifier: an n- epitaxial layer on an n+ substrate with a heavily p-doped anode, rated 1 A / 50 V. The 1N4148 is a planar switching diode: a small npn with a Schottky-clamped base shorted to the cathode, rated 200 mA / 100 V, fast enough for 300 ns recovery. The 1N47xx is a zener: a heavily doped junction with a knee of 2.4-75 V, usually a diffused planar or, in the low-current versions, a temperature-compensated bandgap reference. All three were made by alloying or diffusing junctions into small silicon dice and moulding them in DO-35 glass or DO-41 plastic.

facts.label: 1N4148
facts.value: 200 mA, 100 V, ~4 ns; N planar switching

children.note: The C64 parts list names a rectifier, a switching diode and two zeners on the board, with part numbers. Not established: the internal construction of each (diffused rectifying junction, planar switching junction with a Schottky-clamped base, bandgap-compensated zener) and the current and voltage ratings quoted here. Those are part numbers plus datasheets, and no datasheet is cited.

children.name: Indicator LED (red/green/amber only)
children.description: The C64's power indicator is a 3 mm or 5 mm epoxy-domed LED: a liquid-phase epitaxially grown GaP or GaAsP junction die, die-bonded into a reflector cup on the cathode post, wire bonded to the anode, and encapsulated in a semi-transparent epoxy lens that also acts as a light pipe. Red (GaAsP, ~660 nm) and green (GaP, ~555 nm) were common; amber (GaAsP ~590 nm) and the increasingly cheap GaP red were also in use. Blue LEDs did not exist in 1982 at any price - the first practical blue GaN/InGaN device was 1993, and an efficient one 1995.

children.name: GaP or GaAsP substrate wafer
children.description: The LPE junction layers grow on a polished, Czochralski-grown substrate of n-type or semi-insulating GaAs, or on GaP grown by the same kind of pull used for silicon. GaAs itself is made by liquid-phase or VGF growth from a melt of gallium and arsenic, with the arsenic fed from a boiler of high-purity arsenic metal in hydrogen.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: Czochralski from a Ga/As melt near 1250 C

children.note: GaAs substrate supply was treated as a strategic material in the 1980s; Japan, the USSR and the UK were the main sources.

children.name: Zinc oxide varistor disc
children.description: A MOV disc across the mains input: a disc of ZnO powder mixed with a few percent of glass and pressed and sintered at 1000-1200 C in air. Its resistance is nonlinear - about 1 kohm/mm at low voltage, collapsing to tens of ohms at the 275 V clamping point - because the grain boundaries are thin depleted zinc-oxide grain-boundary phases that break down. Organic or glassy coating and epoxy moulding complete the disc.
places: China (the dominant ZnO supplier by the 1990s)
children.note: ZnO itself comes from zinc concentrate or from the reduction of zinc oxide; that chain belongs in the metals tree. The MOV is in the PSU, not the logic mainboard.

roots.name: U6 2114L colour RAM (1K x 4 static)
roots.description: The C64's screen colour memory at U6, decoding to $D800-$DBE7: 1024 words of 4 bits each, i.e. one colour nibble for each of the 40x25 text screen's 1000 cells. The VIC-II reads these nibbles during the visible portion of every scanline and presents them to the 4-bit colour DAC, so the memory must be fully static with no clocks and no refresh - unlike the eight 4164 DRAMs sitting next to it. Period part numbers are 2114L (MOS Technology / other MOS vendors), MM2114 (National Semiconductor) and plain 2114; the C64 BOM lists 2114L-30, the -30 being a 300 ns speed grade. 18-pin DIP, single +5 V, TTL-compatible bidirectional I/O, about 225 mW.

facts.label: Technology
facts.value: N-channel silicon gate, fully static, no clocks

roots.note: Three corrections to the brief. (1) The part holds 1024 words of 4 bits = 512 bytes, not 1 KB; '1K' refers to the word count, and it is 4 bits wide, not 8. (2) It is not CMOS - the 2114L is explicitly 'N-channel silicon-gate technology', an NMOS cross-coupled inverter latch with a resistor load, not the 6-transistor CMOS cell of later 6264/6280 SRAMs. (3) There was no standard bipolar 4-transistor 2114; the bipolar 1K x 4 memories of the era were unrelated parts (74S287/74S288 and the 74LS189 family are 1K x 1 or 256 x 4). The 'four 256 x 4 or 1K x 4 banks sharing address pins' description does not match the real device: one 1024 x 4 array with ten straight address inputs A0-A9.

children.name: Why static rather than dynamic
children.description: The DRAMs beside it get a refresh cycle roughly every 2 ms because the 6510 can be held off the bus while the KERNAL's refresh routine runs. The colour RAM has no such luxury. The VIC-II fetches a colour nibble out of this chip in the middle of drawing each character cell, within a few hundred nanoseconds of the start of the scanline, from an address counter the VIC owns - there is no software window in which the chip could be taken off to rewrite it. So the cell has to hold its state indefinitely. That is the whole reason for the part: it is a static latch array, and it draws more power (225 mW) than one DRAM chip as a result.

facts.label: Access window
facts.value: a few hundred ns per cell during the visible portion of the scanline

facts.label: Refresh needed
facts.value: none - 'All internal circuits are fully static'

facts.label: Power penalty
facts.value: ~225 mW typ vs ~135 mW for a 4164

children.note: The VIC-II gives about 63 cycles per character cell at 1.02 MHz, roughly 60-70 us of total screen refresh per frame, and it reads one nibble per cell during the ~500 ns the cell is on screen.

children.name: Six-transistor NMOS static cell
children.description: Each of the 1024 nibbles is six transistors: two cross-coupled NMOS inverters forming a bistable latch, plus two NMOS pass transistors that connect the latch to the bit line when the address decoder enables that column. Because it is NMOS, each 'inverter' of the latch is a pull-down transistor in series with a load - which is where the load scheme matters. The latch holds its state for as long as power is applied, with no refresh and no clock, and has to keep roughly 2 V of noise margin at 5 V supply despite sharing a die and a substrate with 1024 other cells that all switch at once.
children.note: The 'six transistors per bit in a typical static RAM' figure is a standard period statement for NMOS SRAM; the cell topology is the classic two-cross-coupled-inverter latch plus two access transistors. Cell layout (single-ended bit line vs differential, and whether the sense amplifier was a shared latch) is not published for the 2114 and is not claimed here.

children.name: The load device: polysilicon resistor or depletion transistor
children.description: This is the real difference between a 2114 and a CMOS SRAM, and it is an extra process step. A ratioed NMOS latch needs something in series with the pull-down transistor to act as a load: on 1982 parts this was typically an undoped or lightly doped polysilicon resistor deposited in the same LPCVD step as the gate, or a depletion-mode NMOS transistor (gate tied to source, threshold deliberately shifted negative by an extra implant) acting as a current source. The depletion option needed one more implant than the resistor option. Not established: which option the C64's 2114 used.

facts.label: Option A
facts.value: undoped polysilicon resistor, 30-100 ohm/sq, no extra mask

facts.label: Option B
facts.value: depletion-mode NMOS load, one extra implant

children.note: Both were standard period practice and the two are visually distinguishable on a die. The specific load device on a 2114L from 1982 is not documented in any available source. Lithium-doped polysilicon was used in some early NMOS logic, but no evidence was found that it was used here.

children.name: Pass transistors and the two-decoder structure
children.description: A 1024 x 4 array is decoded as a 32 x 32 matrix: a six-to-64 row decoder from A0-A5 and a five-to-32 column decoder from A6-A9, each a NAND-type NMOS decoder built from series pull-down strings. Each cell therefore needs two access transistors, one gated by a row line and one by a column line. The decoders are the only clocked-looking part of the chip, but they are combinational - there is no clock input pin at all, which is exactly what makes it static.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 32 rows x 32 columns x 4 bit planes

children.note: A 32 x 32 organisation with two decoders is the natural way to build 1024 x 4 and is what other period 1K x 4 SRAMs used; No published die shot of the 2114 has been seen to confirm the split.

children.name: The 2114 mask set
children.description: Eight or nine 1:1 levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon (gate and, if used, the load resistor pattern), self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad, and alignment/test levels, printed from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment.
children.note: Established: that the colour memory was a bought-in part, so its mask set belonged to a semiconductor vendor rather than to Commodore. The 1992 service manual 326498 parts list gives U6 2114L-30 RAM 901453-01, and its circuit theory states: "Eight 41 64 DRAMS provide 64k bytes of memory. One 2114 RAM (U6) provides 512 bytes of memory allocated for screen color data storage". Not established: the eight-or-nine level count; the level list; the polysilicon load-resistor level; the 1:1 print from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment; and whether the load device on the 2114L was a polysilicon resistor or a depletion transistor, which changes the level count. The 2114 datasheet describes the part electrically and says nothing about how many masks were cut for it.

children.name: How the VIC-II reads it during raster
children.description: The VIC-II owns an internal video address counter that runs ahead of the beam. For each character cell in the visible portion of a scanline it drives the ten colour-RAM address lines and /CS low, and the chip returns the 4-bit colour on D0-D3 within about 300 ns; those four bits go straight to the VIC-II's on-chip 16-colour Y/C generator (mb.vic.palette), which emits them as luminance on pin 15 and chroma on pin 14. When the VIC releases the bus, the 6510 can access the same memory as ordinary RAM at $D800. That single-ended, mid-scanline, few-hundred-nanosecond read is the electrical reason the part had to be a static latch array with roughly 2 V of noise margin.

facts.label: Data path
facts.value: 4 bits direct to the on-chip Y/C generator (mb.vic.palette), bypassing the 6510 data bus

children.note: The VIC-II steals these cycles with AEC low; the CPU sees the colour RAM through $D800 only when the VIC is not driving the bus. Not established: the exact per-cell nanosecond figure, which is consistent with the 2114L-30 300 ns speed grade rather than directly documented, and the ~2 V noise-margin figure.

roots.name: U17 PLA 906114-01 (mask-programmed NMOS)
roots.description: The C64's Programmable Logic Array at U17: it decodes the 6510's address lines and generates the chip-select and bank-switching strobes for every other chip on the board - RAM, ROMs, VIC-II, SID, CIAs, VIA, colour RAM - which makes it the single point of failure for the whole machine. Commodore part number 906114-01, alternate designation MOS 8700-001, die marked MOS 7700R1 / 8700R2. It is a mask-programmed NMOS clone of the Signetics 82S100 bipolar array, in a 28-pin 600 mil epoxy DIP, and it is by far the most failure-prone and most counterfeited part in the machine.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: 16 inputs, 8 tri-state push-pull outputs, 1 output enable

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: MASK programmed at wafer stage - not user-programmable

facts.label: VOH
facts.value: ~3.7-3.8 V (vs 4.2 V for the bipolar Signetics 82S100)

roots.note: Correction to the brief: the part is a 28-pin DIP, not 14 or 16 pin. The 28-pin package is confirmed both by the 'C64 PLA Dissected' reverse-engineering report and by the MOS Technology products list. Also note that early C64s used a bipolar Signetics 82S100 (or Fairchild 93459 clone); the NMOS 906114-01 came later and became the standard part.

children.name: What a PLA physically is
children.description: Two arrays of transistors and a set of 'links'. The fixed AND array is a matrix of diode or transistor junctions arranged so that each row implements one product term - every possible AND of a subset of the 16 inputs. The programmable OR array adds up to eight of those product terms per output. Each product-term-to-output connection is a physical link in that array, and 'programming' the part simply means deciding which links exist. Commodore's version is pure combinational logic with no registered terms, which is why it is fast enough to sit directly on the 6510's address bus and settle inside a 6510 cycle.

facts.label: OR array
facts.value: 8 outputs, each an OR of product terms

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 16, of the 6510's address and control lines

children.note: The 'FE/NE' pin on this package is used for programming field-programmable variants of the device and is left unconnected internally in the mask-programmed 906114-01 - a detail decapping shows.

children.name: Fusible-link and antifuse PLAs
children.description: The two field-programmable routes a PLD could have taken instead, and the reason a mask-programmed part is a different commercial animal. A fusible link is a real wire of chromium or nichrome, 1-3 um thick, burned out by a laser programmer through the package's FE/NE pin - this is how the PAL 16L8 and 20L8 worked, and why a PAL is a catalogue part you can buy in thousands of functions. An antifuse starts as a conducting amorphous-silicon or silicon-dioxide film which a 20-40 V pulse converts into high-resistance insulation; it needs no laser but was slower to program and harder to test. Commodore could use neither for a part sold in the millions at commodity logic prices.

facts.label: Fusible link
facts.value: chromium or nichrome film 1-3 um thick; seconds to program

facts.label: Antifuse
facts.value: amorphous silicon or SiO2 film blown open by a ~20-40 V pulse

facts.label: Mask route
facts.value: 3-6 week cycle from artwork to tested parts; minimum order one wafer run

children.note: The 82S100 that gave the C64 PLA its name was originally marketed as a field-programmable bipolar array of this kind. Whether early C64 82S100 parts arrived pre-programmed from Signetics or were programmed in-house is not established.

children.name: PLA versus PAL: why the name misleads
children.description: The C64's part is called a PLA, but the parts most readers know by that name - the 16L8, 16R8, 20L8 - are PALs, and the two are not interchangeable in sourcing or programming. A PAL is a generic catalogue device: every 16L8 from every vendor is the same silicon, and the buyer programs it. A mask-programmed PLA is a custom device: the buyer cannot program it, and nobody else ever made this function. That is the whole reason fakes are so common - the SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton and PLAtinum parts sold as replacements are typically GAL/EPROM emulations or freshly mask-programmed parts from a third party, and the C64's PLA is precisely the component where a substitute can fail in ways that are hard to trace.

facts.label: PAL 16L8
facts.value: 10 inputs x 8 registered outputs, 64 x 32 fuse AND array, fusible, generic

facts.label: GAL 16V8
facts.value: fuse-programmed, EEPROM fuse link, generic catalogue part
mask programmed, one-off function, no equivalent catalogue part

children.note: Also worth knowing: the 906114 family covered several Commodore machines - 906114-01 for the C64, 906114-04 for the B256, and MOS 8721 (315012-01, 48-pin) elsewhere - but each is a different custom mask.

children.name: Reverse-engineered from a Signetics 82S100
children.description: Early C64s shipped with a bipolar Signetics 82S100, or the Fairchild 93459 clone of it; Signetics was acquired by Philips, which renamed the part PLS100. Commodore's engineers then decapped the bipolar part, photographed it with a Polaroid camera and rebuilt the function as a mask-programmed NMOS design - Bil Herd's recollection is 'We reverse engineered the PLA from Signetics using a polaroid camera'. The resulting die is marked MOS 7700R1 or 8700R2, and it runs at a slightly lower VOH than the bipolar original (about 3.7-3.8 V against 4.2 V), which is part of why early and late C64s behave marginally differently.

children.name: The economics of one custom mask set
children.description: The 906114-01 encodes the entire C64 memory map in a die smaller than the fingertip, and Commodore sold millions of C64s, so once the mask was paid for the part was dirt cheap per unit. But the flip side is that the function exists nowhere else in the world. Any machine needing a different bank-switch map needs a different mask, a different lot and a different lead time - which is why C64Cs needed a different PLA (MOS 8721) to support the cartridge port's new banking. It is also why the cost of a single counterfeit or of a dead original is disproportionate to the value of the silicon inside it.

facts.label: NRE
facts.value: artwork + mask set + verification, once per function

facts.label: Unit cost
facts.value: trivial once masked - the die is tiny and needs no exotic process

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: single-sourced, no drop-in replacement, counterfeiting pressure

children.note: No published figure was found for the specific dollar cost of a mask set in 1982; period sources put a full 8-10 level NMOS mask set in the low tens of thousands of dollars, with mask plates alone a few hundred to a couple of thousand per level.

children.name: Why it fails more than anything else in the machine
children.description: Three reasons stack up. First, it is a single point of failure: if any of its eight strobes misbehaves, the symptom is a dead or misbehaving machine rather than one dead chip. Second, its output enable and eight outputs switch hard on every 6510 cycle against the capacitive load of the whole board, so it is the highest-current part on the bus and the one that sees the worst ringing. Third, and decisively for longevity, it is the one chip that cannot be replaced: a dead 6510 can be bought new; a dead 906114-01 cannot, so in practice a dead PLA means a dead machine unless it is re-masked or emulated.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: 8 push-pull tri-state, switched every CPU cycle

facts.label: Replacement parts
facts.value: SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton, PLAtinum - all substitutes, none original

si.polysilicon.brine.name: Chlor-alkali brine electrolysis
si.polysilicon.brine.description: Salt dissolved in water and electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 3-4 V to make chlorine and hydrogen. The hydrogen is what reduces the trichlorosilane, and the chlorine is one half of the hydrochloric acid that chlorinates the metallurgical silicon in the first place.
si.polysilicon.brine.note: The hydrochloric-acid route is documented: metallurgical-grade silicon is hydrochlorinated to trichlorosilane with hydrogen as a co-product. But the trichlorosilane is then reduced by its own decomposition on hot silicon filaments, not by hydrogen from a chlor-alkali cell, so the claim that cell hydrogen does the reduction is not supported. The cell voltage is also unestablished.

si.polysilicon.gangue.name: Feldspar and mica gangue, hand-picked away
si.polysilicon.gangue.description: The pegmatite that hosts the quartz veins contains albite and K-feldspar with muscovite and biotite. Alumina in feldspar is the enemy - it survives all the way to the aluminium metallisation - so the lump is sorted by hand and by hydrofluoric-acid washing before it is even shipped.
si.polysilicon.gangue.note: Biotite in particular carries a lot of iron and is a classic contaminant marker in a quartz shipment.

si.polysilicon.coke.calciner.name: Delayed coking and calcination of petroleum coke
si.polysilicon.coke.calciner.description: Vacuum residue from crude oil distillation is heated in a battery of delayed-coking heaters to 500 C and held in a large coking drum for 12-24 hours; the green coke is then calcined in a rotary kiln at 1200-1350 C to drive off volatiles and leave needle coke at 0.5-2% sulphur. Silicon furnaces blend petroleum coke with anthracite coal.
si.polysilicon.coke.calciner.note: Not established: the coking-heater temperature, the drum residence time, the calcining-kiln temperature or the sulphur content for any specific producer. Delayed coking and rotary-kiln calcination are standard, but each supplier blends several carbon sources to hit a target ash and sulphur figure that is not published.

si.polysilicon.coke.crude.name: Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled
si.polysilicon.coke.crude.description: Heavy Venezuelan or Middle East crude sent to a vacuum tower at 350-400 C and 30-50 mmHg; the bottoms are a dense black pitch of asphaltenes and metal porphyrins, and are the feed for the coke. Vanadium and nickel concentrate in this residue, so coke made from it carries trace vanadium that the silicon plant has to tolerate.
si.polysilicon.coke.crude.note: Not established: that any particular silicon supplier fed its furnaces with vacuum-residue coke rather than coal-tar pitch, anthracite or low-ash coal, nor the vacuum-tower pressure, the coking-heater temperature or the vanadium figure. Traces of vanadium and nickel in metallurgical silicon, and hence in its carbon reductant, are real, but the level a silicon plant had to tolerate is not a published number.

si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite.name: Anthracite coal as a coke substitute
si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite.description: The other traditional reductant for the submerged arc furnace, mined from the hard coal fields of Pennsylvania, Wales and Shanxi. Lower carbon, higher ash and higher iron than petroleum coke, so it was used as a blend component.
si.polysilicon.coke.anthracite.note: Established: anthracite as a hard, high-carbon, low-impurity coal used in metallurgy. "It has the highest carbon content, the fewest impurities, and the highest energy density of all types of coal and is the highest ranking of coals." and "The carbon content of anthracite is between 86% and 97%." and "Anthracite is categorized into several grades. Standard grade anthracite is used predominantly in power generation, and high grade (HG) and ultra high grade (UHG) are used predominantly in the metallurgy sector." That it served as a carbothermal reductant in a furnace charge is documented for the zinc industry, not for silicon: "The zinc precursors are reduced (carbothermal reduction) by heating with a source of carbon such as anthracite to produce zinc vapor, which is then oxidized as in the indirect process." The 86-97% fixed-carbon range is consistent with a less pure reductant than needle coke, which supports the low-carbon end of the comparison above, but the ash and iron figures are not stated in any source available. Not established: that any specific submerged arc furnace charged anthracite for silicon metal, and in what proportion to petroleum coke; that anthracite was used as a carbon source rather than as fuel; and that Schuylkill County, Glamorgan or Shanxi supplied silicon-grade anthracite. Documented only as coal fields: "The Coal Region of Northeastern Pennsylvania in the United States has the largest known deposits of anthracite coal in the world".

si.cz.crucible-sand.name: Quartz sand melted into crucible glass
si.cz.crucible-sand.description: High-purity quartz sand, acid-leached to remove aluminium and iron, is melted in a flame or arc furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel at about 2000 C into a clear, annealed vitreous silica blank. The graphite is then burnt off in air at 800-1000 C.
si.cz.crucible-sand.note: Not established: how a particular puller supplier made its crucible blank - the acid leach for aluminium and iron, the flame or arc melting around a rotating graphite mandrel, the roughly 2000 C melt and the 800-1000 C burn-off. Standard CZ practice is a high-purity quartz crucible, but the blank-manufacturing route is a supplier trade secret and is not described in any source available here.

si.cz.seed.name: Seed crystal for CZ pulling
si.cz.seed.description: A short (100)-oriented sliver cut from a previous ingot, used to set the orientation and the defect-free growth of the new boule. Its diameter has to match the finished boule, so a seed is cut and ground for each crystal-pulling station.

si.wafer.name: Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
si.wafer.description: The starting substrate every die in the machine is cut from: a 4-inch (100 mm) Czochralski-grown, boron-doped p-type silicon wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, mirror-polished on one face, 300-350 um thick, with a primary flat and a small secondary orientation flat. 125 mm was not standard until about 1986, and by 1982 every logic die in the C64 was patterned on one of these.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 100 mm (4 inch); 125 mm not standard until ~1986

si.wafer.note: Two parts of the machine wanted something slightly different. DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content, because a high bulk oxygen-precipitate density lengthens the trapped-charge lifetime and so helps refresh margin on the 4164. Discrete lines of the era were happy with 10-40 ohm-cm and many of them ran 75 mm wafers, because they did not need fine geometry at all.

si.wafer.slicing.name: Sawing the ingot and laser-scribing the flats
si.wafer.slicing.description: The boule is ground round, a sapphire-orientation-reference crystal is used to find the (100) direction, and the wafer flats are laser-scribed with a ruby or Nd:YAG laser before cutting. Slicing was by OD saw, with blades up to 2.2 m in diameter turning at 2000 rpm for a 0.30 mm kerf, or on more advanced 1982 machines by ID saw, with the blade inside the crystal for a 0.25 mm kerf. The result is a 0.7 mm wafer, far too warped and marked to print on.

facts.label: OD saw
facts.value: up to 2.2 m diameter at 2000 rpm

si.wafer.saw.name: Diamond-impregnated saw blade
si.wafer.saw.description: A thin steel or resin-bonded wheel whose rim carries a diamond grit. Slicing 100 mm silicon at two to three wafers a minute relies on that grit: 20-40 um for a roughing cut and 3-5 um for the finish cut. Resin-bonded blades were introduced in the mid 1970s and gave a thinner kerf and less bow than the metal bond.

facts.label: Blade
facts.value: resin-bonded, OD up to 2.2 m; ID blades inside the boule

si.wafer.saw.note: Not established: the blade diameter, rotational speed, kerf and grit-size figures, or the date on which resin-bonded blades displaced metal-bonded ones. Diamond-wire sawing is the documented modern method; the OD- and ID-saw numbers given here are not in any source available. Kerf and the 0.7 mm as-sawn thickness remain uncertain.

si.wafer.diamond.name: Industrial diamond from graphite
si.wafer.diamond.description: Saw-grade industrial diamond in 1982 was mostly synthetic: graphite pressed and sintered with a diamond-metal catalyst (Fe, Co or Ni) at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press. Natural diamond - the harder, scarcer gem and industrial grade - came from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Botswana and Russia.

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: kimberlite pipe; Gaborone and Kimberley, South Africa

si.wafer.diamond.note: Established: that synthetic diamond was the commercially available source of saw-grade grit well before 1982, and that its first commercial synthesis was a belt process. "Hall achieved the first commercially successful synthesis of diamond on December 16, 1954, and this was announced on February 15, 1955. His breakthrough came when he used a press with a hardened steel toroidal "belt" strained to its elastic limit wrapped around the sample, producing pressures above 10 GPa (1,500,000 psi) and temperatures above 2,000 degC (3,630 degF). The press used a pyrophyllite container in which graphite was dissolved within molten nickel, cobalt or iron. Those metals acted as a "solvent-catalyst", which both dissolved carbon and accelerated its conversion into diamond." The abrasive-versus-gem split is documented in the same passage: "The largest diamond he produced was 0.15 mm (0.0059 in) across; it was too small and visually imperfect for jewelry, but usable in industrial abrasives." Contradicted by that source: the 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C conditions given above sit below the pressures and temperatures recorded for the belt process that made this material commercially available, and the solvent-catalyst metals are specifically nickel, cobalt and iron rather than a generic diamond-metal catalyst. Not established: which maker supplied saw blades to a wafer-slicing shop in 1982; the Kimberley and Botswana kimberlite origins as sources of natural industrial diamond, for which the documented fact is only that natural diamonds are carried to the surface in igneous rocks known as kimberlites; and the Element Six and Sumitomo attributions. That diamond serves cutting and polishing is documented: "Diamond has the highest hardness and thermal conductivity of any natural material, properties that are used in major industrial applications such as cutting and polishing tools."

si.wafer.finish.name: Lapping, chemical polish and edge rounding
si.wafer.finish.description: Saw-cut wafers are lapped double-sided on a rotating cast-iron plate against a conditioning plate, in a slurry of colloidal silica or alumina in water, taking them to about 300 um with several micrometres of total thickness variation left across the wafer. They are then polished chemically in hot alkaline peroxide or in HNO3/HF/acetic acid, which removes the last 10 um or so of saw damage and leaves an atomically flat surface, and finally the razor edge is rounded by a brief hot KOH or NH4OH etch so that photoresist cannot build up on it and so the wafer will not chip in handling.

facts.label: After lapping
facts.value: ~300 um, several um of total thickness variation

facts.label: Polish
facts.value: hot NaOH/H2O2 or HNO3/HF/acetic, removing ~10 um of damage layer

facts.label: Edge
facts.value: rounded in hot KOH or NH4OH

si.wafer.finish.note: Difference from today: a modern wafer goes through CMP in a rotary single-wafer polisher with a soft pad and slurry. Chemical-mechanical polishing did not reach volume production until the late 1980s, so this step was purely chemical in 1982.

si.clean.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
si.clean.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles rather than yield models set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic at 1.6 MHz in deionised water, a hot Piranha of 3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, then RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. Between every mask level the same sequence ran again.

facts.label: Water
facts.value: 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm per die across the whole flow

si.clean.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonic tanks rather than on cassette single-wafer cleaning, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

si.litho.name: Photolithography: coat, bake, expose, develop
si.litho.description: Every layer of every die is defined the same way. The wafer is coated on a spinner at 2000-5000 rpm to 1-3 um of positive photoresist, soft-baked at 90-100 C, aligned to the mask on a 1:1 contact or proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate at 30-50 mJ/cm2, spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard-baked, stripped, and cleaned. Shipley AZ-1350 was the workhorse thin-film resist of the whole industry and the higher-solids AZ-1354 was used wherever the film had to stand up to a deep etch.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1350 thin film, AZ-1354 for thick film

si.litho.note: The step order, the 1:1 contact and proximity print modes, the alkaline developer and the strip chemistry are documented. Not established: the spin speed and film thickness, the bake temperatures, the exposure dose, the AZ-1350 and AZ-1354 resist choices, the Shipley location and the broken-grid alignment scheme giving plus or minus 0.5 um.

si.litho.spinner.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
si.litho.spinner.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer, followed by a convection hot plate or an infrared bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed at a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified nitrogen purge and amber-safe lighting.

si.litho.aligner.name: Contact and proximity mask aligner
si.litho.aligner.description: A 1:1 mask aligner: mercury or xenon source, a 20x-100x binocular microscope, a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and either hard vacuum contact with the mask pressed straight down onto the resist, or a 100-500 um proximity gap. Typical 1982 units were the Coburn 2400, the Kasper 2400, the Universal Exposure Systems machines, and the Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2, whose 5x optical projection removed the "mask lifts off the wafer" failure mode that plagued pure contact printing. Mask work in the 1980s was often done on the same machines, by flashing an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster.

facts.label: Overlay tolerance
facts.value: ~+-0.5 um with a broken-contact or grid-broken layer

facts.label: Typical machines
facts.value: Coburn 2400, Kasper 2400, Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2, UES

si.litho.aligner.note: Named machines are illustrative of the period rather than a documented inventory of the Norristown line. Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, later ASML) were arriving in 1982-83 and were the next generation, not this one.

si.mask.plate.name: Chrome-on-glass photomask plate
si.mask.plate.description: The physical plate a 1982 fab printed from: 5x7 inch of 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz, coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, then exposed and developed in positive photoresist, the exposed chrome etched away in hot perchloric or sulfuric-perchromate acid, washed, inspected on a Zeiss comparison tool against the design database, and defect-repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle. Chromium was the universal absorber from the 1960s onward because of its opacity in the deep UV and its resistance to wet cleaning.

facts.label: Substrate
facts.value: 1 mm soda-lime glass (cheap) or fused quartz (durable), 5x7 inch

si.front-end.name: NMOS silicon-gate front end
si.front-end.description: The flow every simple logic part in the machine ran: n+ source and drain pre-diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 and then wet H2/O2 at about 1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon gate from silane at 800-850 C, a self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant with a 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium sputtered with 0.5-1% silicon and etched in hot phosphoric acid, then PSG and nitride passivation. Ten mask levels, printed 1:1 in AZ-1350 on a contact or Micralign aligner. The 6510 branch under the CPU carries the layer-by-layer version with every temperature; this node is the same flow stated once for the parts that did not need the detail.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: 1-2 um aluminium, single layer, no barrier

si.front-end.note: Difference from today: no refractory barrier metal, no tungsten plug, no CMP-defined metal lines and a single aluminium layer. A static RAM such as the 2114L could run a coarser and older process than the 6510 - there is no tight-pitch sense-amplifier chain to shrink - which is why nothing published states a line width for it.

si.leadframe.name: Stamped DIP lead frame
si.leadframe.description: The die and its leads emerge from a stamped, plated strip. Frames were made from FeNi 42/58 (C4-29) alloy 0.15-0.20 mm thick by progressive die stamping on a 400-800 ton press, then plated - a nickel strike and gold for hermetic parts, or a matte tin or tin-lead plate over nickel for plastic parts. The strip is indexed on a 0.3 inch tape through the bonder and the moulder, and a 40-pin DIP cavity set produces dozens of packaged parts per moulding cycle.

facts.label: Pitch
facts.value: 0.6 inch (15.24 mm) dual row on DIPs; 0.25 inch on TO-92

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: Au over Ni for ceramic; Sn or SnPb over Ni for plastic

si.leadframe.alloy.name: FeNi 42/58 lead frame alloy strip
si.leadframe.alloy.description: The standard low-CTE frame alloy: 42% nickel, 58% iron, with a coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of the die, so the bond survives temperature cycling. Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed to 0.15-0.20 mm. Copper alloy C194 with 2.3% lead, and nickel itself, were the alternatives.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: FeNi 42/58 (C4-29); alternatives Cu C194 with 2.3% Pb, or nickel

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 0.15-0.20 mm after cold rolling and annealing

places: specialty alloy strip mills, US and Japan
si.leadframe.alloy.note: Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed. In 1982 the nickel in it came overwhelmingly from sulphide concentrates - Sudbury in Ontario, the Norilsk-Talnakh massif and the Philippines - won either by the Mond carbonyl loop or by high-pressure acid leach of laterite, then electrolytically refined. The low-carbon steel half came from hematite ore, coke and limestone.

si.leadframe.plating.name: Nickel strike and gold or tin plating of the lead frame
si.leadframe.plating.description: A nickel strike first, because gold will not adhere directly to the iron-nickel alloy and the leads have to solder. Hermetic parts get a heavier gold plate over the nickel; plastic parts get tin or tin-lead over the nickel so the leads solder into the machine's sockets. The bonding tab is always gold-plated, because the die is eutectic-bonded to it.
si.leadframe.plating.note: Not established: the nickel strike, the gold plating of the bonding tab, or the tin and tin-lead plate over nickel for plastic packages. The lead-frame article documents the base alloy (copper, copper alloy or iron-nickel such as alloy 42) and stamping or etching, but not the plating sequence or its thicknesses.

si.emc.name: Silica-filled epoxy moulding compound
si.emc.description: What actually seals a 1982 plastic IC. A thermosetting epoxy or phenolic compound of novolac resin plus 60-75% crushed quartz filler, a small amount of silicone release agent, catalyst and pigment, compounded on a two-roll mill under heat and then transfer moulded at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for one to three minutes, with a post-mould bake at 175 C. A 6510 uses on the order of 0.3-0.5 g of it; a 4164 about 0.1-0.2 g.

facts.label: Cure
facts.value: 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 min; post-mould bake 175 C for 4-24 h

si.emc.note: The same phenolic resin chemistry, in a different form, is the substrate of the C64's own printed circuit board, and the same ground silica filler is in the keyboard's phenolic boards.

si.emc.resin.name: Epoxy novolac resin from phenol and epichlorohydrin
si.emc.resin.description: Phenol and formaldehyde condensed under acid to a novolac resin, which is then reacted with epichlorohydrin and caustic soda to give the epoxy novolac that forms the backbone of the moulding compound. Phenol itself came from cumene-process oxidation of benzene - overwhelmingly a coal-tar derivative in 1982 - or from chlorobenzene hydrolysis.

si.emc.silica.name: Crushed quartz filler from quartz sand
si.emc.silica.description: The single largest mass ingredient in any plastic package: 60-75% by weight of angular fused or ground silica of 0.5-3 um mean size, made by firing and grinding high-purity quartz. It is there to control the shrinkage coefficient and the thermal expansion, and it is why a decapsulated die sits in a white ceramic-looking blob.
si.emc.silica.note: Not established: that silica is 60-75 percent by weight of a 1982 moulding compound, the 0.5-3 um mean particle size, or the shrinkage and expansion-control rationale. The filler fraction is a supplier formulation figure and is not in any source available.

si.attach.name: Die attach to the lead frame
si.attach.simple_name: Die attach to the lead frame
si.attach.description: The die is placed circuit-side-up on a pre-plated gold lead frame tab and swept through a die bonder. The hot-tool bond raises die and frame to about 400-450 C: gold and silicon melt together at 361 C and, on cooling, form a hard Au-Si eutectic weld roughly 25-50 um thick. That is both the mechanical bond and the die's low-resistance thermal path out to the frame. The diced dice are inspected under a stereomicroscope at 20-50x, and under dark-field illumination for particles, before they are attached: a chip on a pad costs the whole package.

facts.label: Alternatives
facts.value: silver-filled epoxy, or glass frit in a ceramic package

si.attach.note: That the die is eutectic bonded to the frame is documented for high-power parts. Not established: the 361 C eutectic temperature, the 3.4 percent silicon content, the 400-450 C tool temperature, the silver-filled organic and conductive-epoxy alternatives, and the incoming-inspection magnification.

si.bond.name: Gold wire wedge bonding
si.bond.description: A wire bonder pulls 25-30 um diameter gold wire from a spool through a ceramic capillary and welds it to the aluminium bond pads: a first wire from each pad out to the frame lead, then interconnect wires pad to pad for internal bussing. Gold is soft, so a wedge-shaped tool presses the wire flat rather than using the ultrasonic ball bond of aluminium bonding. A single 6510 carried about 60 wires, roughly 1.5 m of 25 um gold in total.
si.bond.note: Gold is a documented bond-wire material and wire diameters start below 10 um, which brackets 25 um. Not established: the wire count and length on a 6510, the palladium alloy content, the 0.3-1 m of gold per die, and the gold consumed per year at C64 volumes.

si.mould.name: Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy
si.mould.description: The bonded frame sits in a multi-cavity transfer press and is encapsulated in silica-filled epoxy moulding compound. A typical cycle is 150-180 C at 700-1000 psi for one to three minutes per cavity, and plaques of flash at the parting line are trimmed off in a second press operation. The alternate route for hermetic parts is sintering an alumina ceramic shell at about 850-950 C with a glass frit seal - slower, more expensive, and used for military and aerospace grades.
si.mould.note: Transfer moulding with a pot and plunger forcing compound into a heated cavity is documented. Not established: the 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 minute cycle, the post-mould bake, the flash-trimming second operation, or the 850-950 C glass-frit hermetic alternative.

si.mould.press.name: Hydraulic transfer moulding press
si.mould.press.description: A 50-100 ton multi-cavity transfer press with a heated upper platen, a pot and plunger that pre-form the compound pellet, and the encapsulated lead-frame strip in the cavity. Cycle: close the press, 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, one to three minutes dwell, then open and eject the encapsulated part still on its frame rail.
si.mould.press.note: The pot, plunger and heated cavity of a transfer press are documented. Not established: the 50-100 ton clamping force, the 150-180 C mould temperature, the 700-1000 psi pressure or the 1-3 minute dwell for this era.

si.trim.name: Trim, form, mark and final electrical test
si.trim.description: After moulding the leads are formed on an 8-16 station trim-and-form press - trimmed, bent to the package pitch, flattened, and dipped in a tin or tin-lead solder pot - the body is marked with a dot-matrix ink printer or a Nd:YAG laser with part number, lot code and date code, and the part is dropped into a socket on an automatic tester and run against a final test program.

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: dot-matrix ink (most common in 1982) or Nd:YAG laser

facts.label: Test
facts.value: Teradyne or Fairchild automatic tester in a socket

si.burnin.name: Burn-in and final test
si.burnin.description: Assembled parts were run at elevated voltage - typically 7-9 V on a 5 V part - at 100-125 C for 24 to 168 hours in an oven loaded with sockets on a board, to weed out early-failure parts with contaminated junctions before they reached the customer. The C64 itself needed no burn-in: the chips were simply inserted into the board sockets.
si.burnin.note: Burn-in of consumer-grade MOS parts in 1982 was common but not universal; C64-era Commodore parts often skipped a formal burn-in step.

si.package.ceramic.name: Hermetic ceramic DIP sintering
si.package.ceramic.description: For hermetic parts the die went into a 96% alumina ceramic shell, sealed with a devitrifying glass frit in a belt furnace at about 850-950 C, and the metal flange was brazed or glass-sealed to the header. Ceramic was slower and costlier than plastic and was used for military and industrial grades - but MOS shipped ceramic 40-pin parts of this kind, which is where the collectors' market for them comes from.
si.package.ceramic.note: Dense alpha-alumina is the documented ceramic-package material. Not established: the 96 percent purity figure, the devitrifying glass-frit seal, the 850-950 C belt-furnace sintering, and that MOS shipped ceramic 40-pin parts of this kind.

si.package.ceramic.shell.name: Alumina ceramic DIP shell
si.package.ceramic.shell.description: A 96% alumina header: alumina powder pressed and sintered into a gas-tight body with a metallised cavity floor for the die, a glass-frit seal ring, and a flange carrying the frame leads. Alumina powder comes from bauxite, and that chain lives in the metals and packaging trees.
si.package.ceramic.shell.note: Not established: the 96 percent alumina composition, the pressed-and-sintered route, the metallised cavity floor, the glass-frit seal ring or the flange carrying the leads. Alumina from bauxite is documented, but the header construction is not.

si.probe-card.name: Probe card: gold-plated needles on a printed board
si.probe-card.description: Before dicing, every die is probed on the wafer through a probe card: a fibreglass or ceramic substrate with a pattern of gold-plated tungsten or rhenium needles on 0.1 inch centres, hanging on a probe ring over the die and stepping down with a few grams of force. In 1982 cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated; automatic stepping probe stations were still a novelty at these pad counts.
si.probe-card.note: That die are tested on the wafer before dicing, with binning, by automatic test equipment is documented. Not established: the needle material (tungsten or rhenium), the 0.1 inch needle pitch, the contact force, or that cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated in 1982.

si.package.40.name: 40-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.40.description: The package the 6510 CPU, the 8562 VIC-II and the 6526 CIA shipped in on the C64 mainboard: a 0.6 inch pitch, 40-leaded stamped lead frame with the die eutectic-bonded on its tab, gold wire to the pads, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. A ceramic hermetic version existed for industrial and military customers. The 6581 SID is not in this package: it shipped in a 28-pin DIP, and the service manual's parts list carries 16-pin, 28-pin and 40-pin IC sockets for the board.

facts.label: Compound
facts.value: 60-75 wt% ground silica filled epoxy, ~0.3-0.5 g

facts.label: Marking
facts.value: dot-matrix ink with part number and date code

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: 25 um Au; ~40 pad bonds plus internal bussing

si.package.40.note: Corrected. The 6526 CIA and the VIC-II are documented as 40-pin parts, and the 6510 is a 40-pin part on the C64 board.
