The 6581 SID is not: its pinout ends at pin 28, with the filter capacitors on 26 and 27 and Vdd on 28, so it shipped in a 28-pin package. The service manual names no VIA on this board, so the 6522 has been dropped from the list rather than reclassified. What remains unestablished is the die-attach method, the wire diameter and count, and the moulding-compound figures.

si.package.24.name: 24-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.24.description: The package of the BASIC, KERNAL and character ROMs: a 0.6 inch pitch, 24-leaded stamped lead frame, die eutectic-bonded on its tab, 25 um gold wedge bonding, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. On the C64 mainboard these three were the only chips soldered in rather than socketed, because they cannot usefully be replaced - though owners have socketed them since day one.

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: ~24 pad-to-frame bonds plus a few internal

si.package.18.name: 18-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.18.description: The package of the 2114L colour RAM: an 18-leaded stamped lead frame at 0.6 inch pitch, about 18 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and compound stories are the same as every other DIP in the machine.

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: ~18 pad bonds plus internal wires, 25 um Au

si.package.28.name: 28-pin 600 mil DIP package
si.package.28.description: A wide-body package, because the PLA needs 16 inputs, 8 outputs, an output enable, the unused FE/NE pin, VCC and VSS. Die attach is a gold-silicon eutectic bond on a gold-plated tab, about 28 pad bonds on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, and a transfer-moulded body of silica-filled epoxy, with the leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch in a 28-socket trim-and-form operation. A ceramic variant exists but is uncommon on a C64.

facts.label: Body width
facts.value: 600 mil, 0.6 inch row to row, 28 leads

facts.label: Ceramic variant
facts.value: exists but uncommon on a C64

si.package.8.name: 8-pin plastic DIP package
si.package.8.description: The smallest and most common package in the machine: eight 4164 DRAMs, each a die on an 8-leaded lead frame with about eight frame bonds plus a dozen internal wires for the sense amps, transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy. A 16-pin version of the same die exists for stackable C128 memory.

facts.label: Pinout
facts.value: 1 NC, 2 DIN, 3 /WE, 4 /RAS, 5 A5, 6 A2, 7 A1, 8 VDD

facts.label: Wires
facts.value: 8 frame bonds plus ~8-14 internal, 25 um Au

mb.discretes.led.gallium.name: Refined gallium
mb.discretes.led.gallium.description: Gallium refined from bauxite residue or from zinc residues by repeated ion-exchange in alkaline solution or by amalgam/hydroxide extraction, to 99.9-99.99% metal, then to GaP by reaction with high-purity phosphorus at 1000-1100 C in a sealed quartz ampoule.
mb.discretes.led.gallium.note: Gallium is almost entirely a byproduct of bauxite refining (and of zinc), not a primary ore - this is the same trace metal that makes gallium nitride LEDs possible today. Merged 1982 indicator-LED detail from the peripheral branch: red or amber LEDs of the period were gallium phosphide or gallium arsenide phosphide on a gallium arsenide substrate (GaAs or GaAsP die in an epoxy lens, bandgap about 650-700 nm).

mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.name: Zinc oxide powder from zinc concentrate
mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.description: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed at 900-1000 C to zinc oxide, then reduced with carbon in a shaft or electrothermic furnace at 900-1100 C to zinc metal, burned back to ZnO, and purified to high-purity ZnO for the varistor mix.
mb.discretes.varistor.zinc.note: Established: the carbothermal route to zinc oxide. "The direct or American process starts with diverse contaminated zinc composites, such as zinc ores or smelter by-products. The zinc precursors are reduced (carbothermal reduction) by heating with a source of carbon such as anthracite to produce zinc vapor, which is then oxidized as in the indirect process. Because of the lower purity of the source material, the final product is also of lower quality in the direct process as compared to the indirect one." The reduction temperature is documented too: "ZnO decomposes into zinc vapor and oxygen at around 1975 degC with a standard oxygen pressure. In a carbothermic reaction, heating with carbon converts the oxide into zinc vapor at a much lower temperature (around 950 degC)." That 950 C figure is inside the 900-1100 C range given above; the fluidised-bed roast at 900-1000 C and the shaft or electrothermic furnace are not the documented route, since the documented sequence is reduction to vapour followed by air oxidation. The oxidising step is documented as well: "metallic zinc is melted in a graphite crucible and vaporized at temperatures above 907 degC (typically around 1000 degC). Zinc vapor reacts with the oxygen in the air to give ZnO". Not established: the 900-1000 C fluidised-bed roast; the shaft or electrothermic furnace reduction as described; the burn-back as a separate manufacturing step rather than part of vapour oxidation; and the 50-60% zinc content of run-of-mine sphalerite - the ore is documented as "(Zn, Fe)S", the most important ore of zinc, with iron substituting for zinc, which "can reach up to 40%", so the concentrate grade varies and no fixed percentage applies. Also not established: the Sullivan, Broken Hill and M IDA place names as the sources of a varistor-grade powder, and what makes an electronic-grade ZnO suitable for a varistor. The varistor behaviour itself is documented: the grains sit "in a matrix of other metal oxides, such as small amounts of bismuth, cobalt, manganese oxides", and each grain boundary "forms a diode junction".

mb.cia.test.name: Wafer probe and final test of the 6526
mb.cia.test.description: Probe with a 40-needle card and a program that clocks both 16-bit timers against a reference, steps the serial shift register through a byte, checks the interrupt priority logic and the port handshake, and measures the TOD chain. Assembled parts repeat it in a socket. Because the TOD is clocked from the AC line, the accuracy test needed a calibrated frequency standard, not just a functional pass.

facts.label: Notable check
facts.value: TOD counter accuracy against a frequency standard

mb.cia.test.note: Established: the TOD chain is fed from the AC mains, and the service manual reaches the chip by substitution rather than by test - the 326498 fault table offers Check U1, U15, U7 for no cursor and Check U2, U7 for an intermittent blank screen. Not established: the 40-needle probe card; that the probe program clocked both 16-bit timers against a reference; the shift-register byte step; the interrupt-priority and port-handshake checks; the measurement of the TOD chain; and that the TOD accuracy test needed a calibrated frequency standard. Nothing documents the 6526 wafer probe or final-test regime. The 17-bit counter and the 470 kohm mains feed are documented from the CIA datasheet and the board; the test method above it is not.

mb.color-ram.test.name: Probe, sort and final test
mb.color-ram.test.description: Probed on the wafer with an 18-needle probe card running an address/data checker over all 4096 bits in a marching pattern, then retested after moulding. Because the part has no refresh, its main failure modes are stuck cells from particles and defective decoders, both of which a walking-one/walking-zero pattern catches quickly - which is why the C64's most common colour-RAM symptom, a garbled or shifting character colour, is a die or socket fault rather than a marginal-timing one.
mb.color-ram.test.note: Tester models and exact patterns at Norristown are not documented; the description is the standard period approach to static RAM.

mb.cpu.dicing.name: Die separation: scribe and break, or diamond-wheel saw
mb.cpu.dicing.description: The wafer is flipped onto a vacuum chuck, scored along the scribe lines with a diamond scriber or, in the more expensive method, cut with a resin-bonded diamond wheel on a saw, leaving a kerf of 50-100 um. Small dies like the 6510 (about 3.5 x 3.9 mm) were often diced by scribing and snapping, then washed dry.

children.name: Diamond scriber and dicing saw
children.description: A small die like the 6510 (roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm) was separated either by scoring the wafer's back-side scribe lines with a diamond scriber and snapping the wafer along them, or by cutting with a resin-bonded diamond wheel leaving a 50-100 um kerf. The wafer was then washed dry, and a final microscopic inspection checked each die's edges and surface before it went to bonding - a chip on a pad would cost a whole package.

facts.label: Coolant
facts.value: deionized water or a solvent jet

mb.cpu.front-end.name: 2 um NMOS front end: the layer stack
mb.cpu.front-end.description: A silicon-gate, double-polysilicon NMOS process flow on p-type (100) CZ silicon: heavily doped n+ source/drain first, LOCOS field oxide, heavily n-doped polysilicon gate, self-aligned arsenic source/drain, contact cuts, aluminium metallization, then phosphosilicate glass plus a plasma nitride seal. Ten mask levels, ~50 major process steps, roughly 6-8 weeks of fab cycle time.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: single aluminium level, single poly gate + poly load resistor

mb.cpu.front-end.note: Layer thicknesses for the specific 6510 are reconstructed from period NMOS design rules, not from a published process manual. There was exactly ONE metal layer - no aluminium barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP, no dual damascene. The whole flow ran in class 100 bays of the Norristown plant, fed by fan filter units over a class 1000 corridor at 70% RH and +-1 C, with nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen distributed on stainless panels from bulk tanks.

children.name: 1. n+ source/drain pre-diffusion
children.description: A thermal phosphorus diffusion: the wafer is coated with a phosphosilicate glass (PSG) doped by PH3 or by a PBN (pyrolytic boron nitride) solid phosphorus source, then held at 900-950 C for 30-60 minutes to push phosphorus about 0.5-1 um into the silicon. The result is a heavily doped (10^20 cm^-3) n+ region that will become the bit-line/tap contact landing areas and the bases of the load and driver devices.
children.note: Some 1982 fabs used an arsenic implant instead of phosphorus diffusion; Norristown is documented only as an NMOS shop, not at this level of detail.

children.name: 2. LOCOS field oxide
children.description: The active-area mask is defined in photoresist over the grown oxide, and field oxide grown by two-step thermal oxidation: a dry O2 pass at ~1000 C to lay down the thin masking oxide, then steam at the same temperature for ~2 hours to reach 6000-8000 A of field oxide. Field oxide was the isolation, the mask for the self-aligned source/drain implant, and the thickest feature on the die.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: dry O2 then wet H2/O2, 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Bird's beak
facts.value: ~1-2 um lateral encroachment - the reason a field-gate design was attractive

children.note: LOCOS was still the isolation scheme in 1982; trench isolation was a few years away.

children.name: 3. Deposition and doping of the polysilicon
children.description: Polysilicon was deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition in a heated-wall tube furnace from silane (SiH4) at 800-850 C or from dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) at ~1000 C, giving 4000-8000 A of polycrystalline film. For gates it was deposited heavily n-doped in the same step by adding phosphine to the silane flow. Undoped poly, or lightly doped poly, was also deposited in the same furnace as the load resistors and as the depletion-mode loads the 6510 datasheet describes.
children.note: Dichlorosilane was cheaper per deposited atom than silane and preferred for thick films, but carried chlorine that required a careful post-deposition clean.

children.name: 4. Poly gate oxidation (the real '3.5 V' gate dielectric)
children.description: After the undoped polysilicon is patterned, the whole wafer is re-oxidised: the bare silicon is left capped by the 400 A screen oxide, while the poly itself grows its own oxide. Dry O2 at 1000-1100 C for 30-90 minutes grows ~350-450 A of silicon dioxide on the poly, converting it into a depletion-mode MOSFET with the same gate dielectric as the silicon. This is why 'the gate oxide was grown in an oxygen furnace' is literally true of silicon-gate NMOS - but on the poly, not on the channel.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 350-450 A (~800 A grown to allow for later poly oxidation)

children.name: 5. Self-aligned source/drain implant
children.description: With the poly gate and field oxide standing up, the wafer is ion-implanted with arsenic (or phosphorus) at 50-150 keV. The gate poly and the field oxide act as their own masks, so the source and drain edges are formed automatically under the poly edges with no alignment tolerance at all. The implanted arsenic is then annealed at 1000-1100 C in dry O2 or N2, which also drives it under the gate edge and repairs implant damage.

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: self-alignment is what made 2 um silicon-gate NMOS practical in a small fab

children.name: 6. Contact cut and aluminium metallization
children.description: Contact windows are cut in the field oxide with an HF dip masked by photoresist (silicon dioxide etches fast in HF), then the wafer is coated by vacuum evaporation or DC sputtering with 1-2 um of aluminium containing 0.5-1% silicon to stop aluminium spikes punching through thin junctions. The aluminium is patterned by a hot phosphoric-acid etch (H3PO4:HNO3:acetic acid/water at ~50-80 C) or, from the late 1970s, by a CF4/O2 plasma in a barrel etcher.
children.note: Difference from today: no refractory barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP-defined metal lines, and a single aluminium layer - the die simply had no room for more.

children.name: 7. Passivation and pad opening
children.description: The aluminium is sealed under a phosphosilicate glass overcoat grown by CVD from TEOS and phosphine at 700-800 C, and in 1982-84 plants increasingly by plasma-enhanced CVD silicon nitride (~700 C, SiH4/NH3 or SiCl4/NH3 in a low-frequency glow discharge). Pad windows are opened with a hot phosphoric acid etch of the nitride followed by a buffered HF dip.
children.note: Whether the 6510 die carried nitride passivation or only PSG is not publicly documented; nitride passivation at a small internal fab in 1982 is plausible but not certain.

children.name: Positive photoresist: spin, soft-bake, expose, develop
children.description: Wafer coated on a spinner (2000-4000 rpm) to 1-2 um of AZ-1350, dried 90-100 C for 20-30 min on a hot plate, aligned to the mask in a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 optical proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate, then spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. Between every step: megasonic clean, dilute H2SO4:H2O2, and a hard bake.
children.note: The contact and proximity print modes, the roughly 5 um proximity gap and the alkaline tetramethylammonium hydroxide developer are documented. Not established: the AZ-1350 resist and its thickness, the 90-100 C bake, the Coburn 2400 and Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 model numbers, and when 10x reduction steppers became available.

children.name: Oxidation and diffusion tube furnaces
children.description: Quartz or fused-silica tube furnaces, horizontal, 5-6 inch ID, with 2-4 zone radiant or resistance heating to 1100 C, a boat of silicon-carbide or quartz carrying 25-50 wafers, and gas flow panels with wet/dry mixing valves. These did the field oxide, gate oxide, poly anneal and the source/drain drives.

children.name: Polysilicon LPCVD furnace and aluminium sputterer
children.description: A second tube furnace, plumbed for silane/phosphine or dichlorosilane, for poly deposition. Aluminium went on in a separate vacuum tool: a DC magnetron sputter chamber (Balzers, Perkin-Elmer, Leybold) or a resistive evaporation chamber, both with turbomolecular pumps and a rotary fixture.

children.name: Wet etch bench and plasma etcher
children.description: Wet etches in quartz or PVDF tanks: HF for oxide, hot H3PO4 for aluminium, buffered oxide etch (HF:NH4F) for fine oxide patterning. By 1982 many fabs had added a barrel-type CF4/CF4+O2 plasma etcher (e.g. the Plasma Technologies PT etch, or an ASM) for aluminium and for poly etching.
children.note: Established: wet-chemical patterning of oxide and aluminium with HF and hot phosphoric acid, and the buffered HF/NH4F oxide etch, are documented period practice for a 1982 silicon-gate NMOS line. Not established: whether Norristown owned a plasma etcher at all in 1982, whether the CF4 or CF4+O2 chemistry was used here or only for poly, the barrel-versus-downstream configuration, and the Plasma Technologies PT or ASM machines, whose names are illustrative of the period rather than a documented inventory. Also not established: the quartz or PVDF tank material.

children.name: Low-energy ion implanter
children.description: A small Van de Graaff or mass-separated implant source (High Voltage Engineering, Extrion, or Veeco) accelerating arsenic to 50-150 keV, with a beam scanning and dose measurement unit. Implantation of the source/drain had largely replaced diffusion by 1982 in a well-equipped shop.
children.note: If Norristown did not own an implanter, this step was done as an outside foundry service - plausible for a small internal fab, but undocumented.

mb.cpu.probe.name: Wafer probe (electrical die sort)
mb.cpu.probe.description: Before dicing, each die is probed on a wafer with a probe card: a printed-circuit board with 40 microscopic tungsten or rhenium needles, one per 6510 bond pad. A Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST automated tester drives a test program and logs wafer coordinates, so only known-good dice go to assembly. Probe cards in 1982 were hand-drilled needle cards; automatic stepping probes were still rare.
mb.cpu.probe.note: That die are probed on the wafer by automatic test equipment, with binning, before dicing is documented. Not established: the 40-needle tungsten or rhenium card, the Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST models, the wafer-coordinate logging, or that stepping probe stations were rare in 1982.

mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication.name: Cutting, inspecting and repairing the mask plates
mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication.description: The 6510 layout existed as polygons on a Calma or Computervision workstation. It was checked against the design rules, extracted to a mask database and written to tape, and a mask data preparation program merged the layout with the process layers, the alignment marks and the die boundary to produce the flat rectangle-and-trapezoid format the pattern generator consumed. The generator then flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or a 1:1 mask writer exposed the blank plate directly. Each plate was developed in positive resist, the exposed chrome etched away, inspected on a Zeiss or KLA comparison tool against the database, and defect-repaired with a gallium or indium needle or by lifting and re-exposing the film. This data-reduction step, not the exposure, was where most mask errors were caught.

facts.label: Layout system
facts.value: Calma or Computervision, magnetic tape in and out

facts.label: Output
facts.value: rectangle/trapezoid tape for the pattern generator

facts.label: Inspection
facts.value: Zeiss or KLA comparison tool against the design database

facts.label: Repair
facts.value: gallium or indium needle, film lift and re-expose, or deposited carbon

mb.cpu.mask-set.fabrication.note: Whether Norristown used an in-house plotter, bought plates from a regional mask shop, or mixed the two is not documented in any public source. Electron-beam mask writers existed by this date but at roughly US$1-2 million they were not typical in a device plant this size.

children.name: Pattern generator driving a mask exposure
children.description: In 1982 most masks of this size were made by a numerically controlled pattern generator that flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or by a 1:1 mask writer that exposed a blank plate directly. Electron-beam mask writers (EBG, Santa Clara) existed but at roughly US$1-2 million were not typical in a small internal device fab.
children.note: Whether Norristown used an in-house plotter, a purchased mask from an outside mask shop, or a mix is not documented in public sources.

children.name: Mask inspection and defect repair
children.description: Masks were checked on a Zeiss or KLA comparison mask inspection tool against the design database, printing defect-free chrome checkouts. Opaque defects on clear areas were repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle or by lifting the film and re-exposing; clear defects in a chrome line were patched with deposited carbon. Pellicles - 1-2 um Mylar membranes mounted in a frame - protected final production masks from dust, though they were less common for 1:1 contact printing, where the mask still touched the wafer. Inspection was the last gate before a plate went into the mask library, because one bad plate silently ruins a whole wafer run.
children.note: A 1 um defect on a 2 um feature is not something the process can tolerate, which is why mask repair was routine work rather than an exception.

mb.discretes.bjt.name: Planar epitaxial small-signal BJT process
mb.discretes.bjt.description: The 2N3904, 2N3906 and 2N4124 are all the same architecture, differentiated by polarity and voltage rating: a p-type substrate, a heavily arsenic- or phosphorus-doped n+ subcollector, then a 1-3 um epitaxial n collector layer grown in an ATCP radiant-heated reactor at ~1150-1250 C with AsH3 or PH3 in H2. Isolation diffusions of boron create the tub, then the base (boron, ~0.5-1 um deep) and finally the emitter (arsenic or phosphorus, heavily overdoped to a low base resistance) through separate photolithography steps. Aluminium metallization is deposited by evaporation, alloyed at 400 C to make ohmic contacts, then the wafer is probed.

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: arsenic or phosphorus, ~97% of emitter area (GEOR)

facts.label: 2N3904 rating
facts.value: 40 V VCEO, 200 mA Ic, 625 mW Pd

facts.label: 2N3906 rating
facts.value: complementary PNP, 40 V, 200 mA, ~250 MHz fT

mb.discretes.bjt.note: Motorola registered the 2N3904/2N3906 in the mid-1960s as a pair, which is why almost every 1982 household electronics catalog lists them as Motorola parts even when another firm made them.

mb.discretes.epi.name: Radiant-heated epitaxial reactor
mb.discretes.epi.description: After the n+ subcollector diffusion, a 1-3 um n-type epitaxial layer was grown in a radiant-heated vertical reactor: the wafers sat on a graphite susceptor inside a quartz bell jar, inductively heated to 1150-1250 C, with AsH3 or PH3 in H2 flowing over them. Epitaxy gave the collector the uniformity and the carrier concentration that a diffusion simply could not, which is what made the 2N3904's gain and its saturation voltage repeatable.
mb.discretes.epi.note: Not established: the reactor geometry (radiant-heated vertical, graphite susceptor in a quartz bell jar), the inductive coupling, the 1150-1250 C setpoint or the 1-3 um epitaxial thickness. Epitaxial growth of a doped layer on a crystalline seed is documented in general; the reactor description is not.

mb.discretes.isolation.name: Isolation diffusion and its moat
mb.discretes.isolation.description: A boron diffusion deep enough to reach the subcollector creates a p-type tub around each transistor, isolating it from its neighbours through reverse-biased pn junctions rather than an oxide. The same oxide that covers the tub is later cut away in the base and emitter windows - this is the 'planar epitaxial' process invented at Fairchild in 1959 and still the standard discrete recipe in 1982.

mb.discretes.test.name: Probe, gain binning and final test of the discretes
mb.discretes.test.description: Discretes are probed on the wafer with a 3- or 10-needle card, then tested after packaging on a curve tracer or a dedicated bin tester. Bipolar small-signal parts are binned by hFE and by VCEO - the 2N3904's hFE spread runs roughly 100-300 - so a given lot is graded, and the C64's assembly only ever saw parts within the standard bin. Rectifiers are tested for reverse leakage and forward drop at rated current.
mb.discretes.test.note: That wafer-level binning by automatic test equipment is standard practice is documented. Not established: the 3- or 10-needle card, the hFE and VCEO grade bands, the 100-300 hFE spread at a stated bias, or that gain binning rather than lot screening was what the C64 assembly received.

mb.discretes.led.epi.name: Liquid-phase epitaxy of the GaP junction
mb.discretes.led.epi.description: A GaP or GaAsP wafer is dipped in a molten, boron-doped Ga/GaP/P solution in a horizontal tilting boat inside a long quartz tube furnace at ~850-900 C. The substrate is swept through many alternating supersaturated melts so that dozens of GaP layers a few microns thick grow in, alternating p-type (Zn-doped) and n-type (S-doped) to form the double-heterostructure junction that makes the bright 1980s LED. The process is epitaxial in the strict sense - it is the same technique used for GaAs microwave chips.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: quartz tube with tilting boat and zone pulls

mb.discretes.led.epi.note: Liquid-phase epitaxy is the documented route for the bright GaAsP/GaP junction of this period, and the double heterostructure came from it. Not established: the 850-900 C melt temperature, the boron-doped Ga/GaP/P charge, the alternating-supersaturation sweep, or the zinc and sulphur dopants as such. Gallium phosphide is documented as dissociating above about 900 C and being grown from a 1500 C melt, which does not match the temperature given here.

mb.pla.mask-programming.name: Mask programming of the link pattern
mb.pla.mask-programming.description: This is the practical heart of a mask-programmed PLA. The AND array, the OR array and the decoders are all routine NMOS layers, but the pattern of which links exist is frozen into a single additional mask level - drawn as one extra colour plane in the layout database and cut like any other plate. That one extra mask is what makes each unique logic function expensive: artwork generation, mask fabrication and inspection all have to be repeated, and the wafer run cannot be short because the lot must be big enough to be worth the NRE. The whole array is physically small, so a 4-inch wafer holds many thousands of dies - the constraint on order size is mask and engineering cost, not silicon.

facts.label: Revisions
facts.value: each logic change costs a whole new mask set

facts.label: Programming step
facts.value: none: every 906114-01 off the line is already a C64 address decoder

facts.label: Where the cost sits
facts.value: non-recurring engineering, paid once per unique logic function

mb.pla.mask-programming.note: This is the mechanical reason the 906114-01 is unreplaceable in practice: there is no second source, no substitute function, and no way to change the logic without new silicon.

mb.pla.process.name: NMOS process for the 906114-01 (node not claimed)
mb.pla.process.description: The device-level facts are solid: it is NMOS, mask programmed, made at Norristown, and running a lower VOH than the bipolar original. The process details are not published anywhere. On the evidence of die markings, the era and the same fab, it is almost certainly the house silicon-gate NMOS flow used for the 6510, 6522 and 6526 - n+ diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, LPCVD polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, one aluminium layer, PSG or nitride passivation - run at whatever line width that flow was at the time. No specific figure is asserted for that line width, because no source states one for this part.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: aluminium; no barrier metal in this period

mb.pla.process.note: Explicitly low confidence and deliberately vague. The 906114-01's internal process has never been documented; inferring it from the rest of the CSG part family is an assumption, not a fact. What is not in doubt is the programming mechanism, which is the point of this branch.

mb.pla.test.name: Probe, truth-table test and final test
mb.pla.test.description: A PLA is uniquely testable because its specification is a truth table rather than a waveform. On probe, a stored truth table is stepped through all 16 inputs x /OE combinations on all 8 outputs - a few thousand vectors - which catches a stuck link, a shorted link or a bad decoder in seconds. Assembled parts get the same vector set in a socket on an automatic tester, plus a timing check that the address decode settles inside a 6510 cycle.
mb.pla.test.note: Not established: the probe-card pin count, the vector count, the 3-6 week cycle, or that exhaustive truth-table testing was standard practice for mask-programmed PLDs. The device has 16 inputs and 8 outputs, so an exhaustive test is arithmetically small, but no source describes the test regime.

mb.ram.process.name: Two-level polysilicon NMOS DRAM process
mb.ram.process.description: Same basic silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU but heavier: thicker field oxide, more polysilicon depositions (three), a heavier arsenic source/drain, a thicker aluminium (2-3 um) for the bit lines that have to survive repeated bootstrapped swings, and usually two mask levels for bit-line precharge and sense amp. Eight to ten mask levels and 100-150 process steps, versus ~50 for the CPU.
mb.ram.process.note: DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content than logic wafers: a high bulk oxygen-precipitate density lengthens the trapped-charge lifetime and so buys refresh margin on a 64K part. That is the one place the 4164 substrate differs from the 6510's. Established: only the substrate-oxygen rationale above. Not established: the 8-10 mask, 100-150 step, 2-3 um aluminium and 60-100 day figures; no datasheet is cited.

children.name: Projection printing the poly 2 and bit-line levels
children.description: The tight overlays in a 4164 (bit line over capacitor plate, poly 2 over poly 1) were what finally forced 5x reduction step-and-repeat printing rather than 1:1 contact printing, because 1:1 contact printing of a 4 um bit line over a 4 um plate feature was too lossy. Typical 1982 DRAM mask lines ran GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers, with hard-baked 2 um Shipley AZ-1354 resist and a 5x reticle on a 3x3 inch quartz plate.
children.note: Some 64K DRAMs were still made on 1:1 proximity aligners in 1981-82; by 1984 5x steppers were standard across the industry.

mb.ram.protection.name: Alpha-particle and latch-up protection
mb.ram.protection.description: DRAM soft errors from alpha particles emitted by radon daughters in the mould compound were a real field-failure mode in 1982. Mitigations used then: a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride chip cover potted over the die in a hermetic package; 'getter' compounds in the cavity; and softer, minimum-area bit-line and capacitor geometries to increase the stored charge margin.

facts.label: Alpha energy
facts.value: ~5-6 MeV from Rn-222 progeny in the epoxy

facts.label: Typical soft error rate
facts.value: ~1 FIT to 100 FIT per device, highly variable

mb.ram.protection.note: The IBM/Samsung 'HAB' (hit-point-address-bypass) and soft-error work of the mid 1980s came later.

children.name: Sintered chip cover over the die
children.description: On many 64K DRAMs the mould compound was not allowed near the die: instead a small alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead frame cavity and the cavity then filled with a low-alpha moulding compound or left in a hermetic ceramic package. Alpha emission rate of the compound was a purchased specification in units of alphas per cm2 per hour.
children.note: Established: nothing about this part is documented for any 4164 fitted to a C64. The 1992 service manual mentions no cover pot, ceramic package, lid or alpha specification anywhere in its text or its 326498 parts list, where the 4164 appears as an ordinary moulded DIP at U9-U12 and U21-U24, part 901505-01. Not established: that a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead-frame cavity on any of these parts; that the cavity was then filled with a low-alpha compound or left hermetic; the single-ended-versus-differential sense path; and the under 0.04 alpha per cm2 per hour figure, which is a purchased supplier qualification limit rather than a value in any C64 parts list. Alpha-particle soft errors in DRAMs are documented in general; the specific mitigation used on these dies is not, and no die photograph or teardown of a 4164 has been used here.

mb.ram.sort.name: Wafer sort and final test of the 4164
mb.ram.sort.description: Every die is probed with an 8-needle probe card and tested on an automated memory tester that runs a march-type pattern (write a checkerboard, read it, invert, repeat) through all 65,536 cells, then a refresh test holding 128 RAS cycles. Assembled parts go back into a socket on the same tester for a signature/AC timing check at 150 ns. Timing bins came out of this test - the C64 does not need the fastest grade, but the drive and the C128 memory expansions did.

facts.label: Testers
facts.value: Teradyne L-200, Fairchild SICTEST, or a Voltronik 5n

mb.ram.sort.note: Specific tester models are typical of the period; the ones at Norristown or at the Asian vendors are not documented.

mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.name: Second polysilicon layer: the storage capacitor
mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.description: The key DRAM process problem in 1982. A second conformal polysilicon layer had to be deposited and patterned so that its edge was razor sharp and its overlap onto the access transistor was tight. Deposition was LPCVD silane at ~800-850 C; the plate was doped n+ with a phosphorus implant and annealed. Refractory metal silicides (WSi2, TiSi2) were being introduced on gates in 1983-84 but were not universal in 1982 64K DRAMs.
mb.ram.cell.doublepoly.note: Polysilicon is documented as the gate material deposited by LPCVD and doped in the same step with phosphine. Not established: that the storage node is a second conformal polysilicon plate, the 800-850 C deposition, the 3000-5000 A thickness, or the 1983-84 arrival of tungsten and titanium silicides. The second-layer polysilicon plate is not described in the sources available.

mb.roms.process.name: NMOS mask ROM front end
mb.roms.process.description: The same silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU - n+ source/drain diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, 1-2 um aluminium, PSG/nitride passivation - with one extra mask level for the ROM programming pattern. A 24-pin DIP ROM die is small (a few mm2) and yields well; the constraint was mask cost, not yield.
mb.roms.process.note: Not established: the mask level count for a mask ROM (eight plus one programming level), the claim that the constraint was mask cost rather than yield, or that the ROM die is small enough to yield well. A mask-programmed ROM is one extra mask level above the same NMOS front end, but no source gives the level count for these parts.

mb.roms.programming.name: Mask programming: one mask set per ROM revision
mb.roms.programming.description: An NMOS mask ROM of 1982 was an NMOS transistor array with a decoder, programmed by removing or adding contacts/metal at the array intersections. The usual 1980s implementation was contact programming: the programmer and sense-amp metal were left unconnected at a bit=1 location, and the ROM-only mask plate was drawn with those contact cuts simply omitted - or, in the opposite polarity, extra contact cuts were added for every 0. The array is arranged 32 bit lines (or 24, using 6 cells of 4 transistors) across 2048 words for the 8 KB parts.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 2048 words x 8 bits for 8 KB; 512 x 8 for 4 KB

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: contact / via programming done as an edit to one mask

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: each ROM revision = a new mask set cut and a new process run

mb.roms.programming.note: Two other read-only technologies sat alongside the mask ROM in the same decade and neither is what Commodore used: a thin-film PROM stores the bit as a sheet of 25-200 ohm/sq nichrome (Ni80/Cr20) or Cr-SiO2 cermet, sputtered or co-evaporated and then programmed by laser or sand-blast ablation through a resist. The mask ROM is a transistor array with one extra mask, which is exactly why a ROM revision costs a whole wafer run.

children.name: Bit-line sense amplifiers
children.description: A masked bit line is precharged high and then a dummy word is selected to develop a voltage across the bit line; a differential sense amplifier (a latch of four NMOS transistors plus a pair of cross-coupled load devices, exactly the same topology as the 6510's logic) amplifies the millivolt difference and latches it. The sense amps were the largest block in a mask ROM die - typically 10-15% of the area - because each needed a perfect match.

facts.label: Signal
facts.value: a few mV differential, amplified to a full logic swing

children.note: Established: only the identity of the parts. The 1992 service manual 326498 parts list gives U3 as 2364 Basic ROM C 901226-01 and U4 as 2364 Kernal ROM C 901227-03. Not established: the precharge-and-develop read scheme; the four-transistor-plus-load differential sense amplifier; the 10-15 percent of die area figure; and the few-millivolt differential signal. No source describes the internal circuit of either Commodore mask ROM, and no die photograph or decapping of a 901226-01 or 901227-03 has been used. A precharged bit line read by a differential sense amplifier is standard period NMOS mask-ROM practice, but which sense-amplifier topology these two parts used is not established, nor is the claim that the sense amplifiers were the largest block on the die.

mb.roms.verify.name: Verifying every ROM bit
mb.roms.verify.description: A mask ROM cannot be re-programmed, so its contents are verified twice. On the wafer, a 24-needle probe card runs a read-only pattern through the 8192 or 4096 addresses and sums the data; after assembly, the part goes into an automatic tester that reads the whole array and checks it against a resident signature and, for the C64's BASIC and KERNAL, the published checksum. Any failure meant a defective mask or a contamination particle, and the whole mask set had to be re-run.
mb.roms.verify.note: Not established: the 24-needle probe card, the 0.1 inch pin pitch, the read-only sum of the whole array, or the published checksum comparison for BASIC and KERNAL. That a ROM die is verified on the wafer by automatic test equipment and again after assembly is the documented practice.

mb.sid.process.name: NMOS hybrid process: digital counters on an analogue poly
mb.sid.process.description: The 6581 was not a purely digital NMOS part. Its 24-bit phase accumulators, the noise LFSR and the envelope generators are ordinary silicon-gate NMOS with depletion loads, the same technology as the 6510. Its DACs, the filter and the VCA are analogue: long polysilicon resistors laid down in the same polysilicon deposition, a large-area common-emitter output transistor, and a big p-diffused 'pump' resistor in the VCA. All of it in one 2-4 um process with a single aluminium layer, and with the analogue section laid out shielded inside its own p-epitaxial tub.

facts.label: DAC
facts.value: R-2R style, built from polysilicon resistors and n+ lands

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: p-type epitaxial tub around the analogue block

mb.sid.process.note: The poly-resistor DAC and the tub isolation are standard period NMOS-analogue practice (Hitachi, Toshiba, Signetics used exactly this) but the internal details of the Norristown 6580/6581 are not public.

mb.sid.test.name: Wafer probe and audio test of the 6581
mb.sid.test.description: Probe testing a SID meant electrical tests (register access, oscillator counters, envelope thresholds, DAC linearity, filter self-oscillation) plus, on the better lines, a functional audio test: a short score stepped through the chip and the output listened to or measured on a spectrum analyser. Final test repeated it in a socket. This is why 6581 revisions are dated and marked (R4, R4AR, R5, R6) - each was a measured change to the analogue thresholds. The threshold voltages of the envelope generators and the VCA had to be trended, because the whole reason the 8580 sounds different is that its analogue section was redesigned and its thresholds tightened.
mb.sid.test.note: Established: that the 6581 was supplied in dated, revision-marked forms. The 1992 service manual 250466-01 C64-B3 parts list carries LSI SID 6581 R3 under Commodore number 906112-01, and the 250469-01 C64-E list carries the 8580 as U9 318013-01, so an R-suffix on the part number is documented practice at Commodore. Not established: the 40-needle probe card; that a functional audio test played a short score through the chip and measured the output on a spectrum analyser; that envelope and VCA threshold voltages were trended; and the claim that each revision was a measured change to the analogue thresholds discovered on probe. That die are probed on the wafer before dicing, with binning, by automatic test equipment is documented period practice. No source describes the 6581 electrical test program, its analogue coverage, or how the filter and envelope thresholds were controlled in production.

mb.vic.process.name: NMOS front end for a large analog-plus-logic die
mb.vic.process.description: The same silicon-gate NMOS sequence as the CPU, with extra care because the VIC-II mixes digital logic, the fixed-palette analogue section and comparators on one die: 2 um minimum feature, ~400 A poly-oxide, LOCOS field oxide, self-aligned n+ source/drain, single 1-2 um aluminium layer, PSG plus plasma nitride passivation. The analogue section generates the fixed 16 luminance and chrominance levels on-chip, with resistor values shared between opposite hues to save die area, and emits them on pins 14 and 15.
mb.vic.process.note: Exact die size and mask count for the 8562 are not published; 50-60 mm2 is an estimate from the pin count and function. Not established: the exact analogue output transistor structure and the on-die resistor values.

mb.vic.test.name: Wafer probe and pattern test of the 8562
mb.vic.test.description: The VIC-II is probed with a 40-needle card and a test program that exercises the character generator, the sprite pointers, the colour registers and the interrupt logic - and, on the analogue side, checks the two video outputs (luminance on pin 15, chroma on pin 14) and the colour-register decode. Assembled parts run the same program in a socket, often while a technician watched a test pattern on a monitor plugged into the tester's video output.

facts.label: Die size
facts.value: large relative to a 6510, so yield-sensitive

mb.vic.test.note: Established: that the chip is a Commodore first-party part and how the service manual diagnoses it - the 326498 parts list gives U19 6567 VIC II C 906109-04, and the fault table for a blank screen on power up lists U19 (VIC II) among the parts to check. Not established: the 40-needle probe card; that the probe program checked that all six colour outputs swung the full 0-5 V; that all eighteen colour latches were decoded at probe; that a technician watched a test pattern on a monitor plugged into the tester video output; and the die-size comparison against the 6510. The 8562 die area is not published, and the 50-60 mm2 figure used elsewhere in this branch is an estimate. That die are probed on the wafer before dicing, with binning, by automatic test equipment is documented period practice; nothing documents the VIC-II probe program or its analogue coverage.

mb.sid.poly-res.name: Polysilicon load resistors
mb.sid.poly-res.description: The 6510 and the SID both use undoped or lightly doped deposited polysilicon as a resistor, deposited in the same LPCVD silane step as the gate and left unetched between two aluminium contacts. Sheet resistance was 30-100 ohm/sq in 1982 and the resistance was trimmed, if at all, by laser or by anodising the surface - the 'thin-film resistor' trimming industry existed for exactly this.

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~+0.1 to +0.3 %/C - poor by modern thin-film standards

mb.sid.poly-res.note: Silicon-barrier anodes, nitride barriers and copper lines did not exist; a 1982 IC resistor could drift several hundred ppm per year with humidity.

si.wafer.diamond.grit.name: Industrial diamond grit (saw-grade)
si.wafer.diamond.grit.description: Synthetic saw-grade diamond grit for wafering saws, dice tools and grinding wheels. Graphite pressed and sintered with Fe/Co/Ni catalyst at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press; the largest early stones were 0.15 mm across, too small for jewelry but usable in industrial abrasives. Grit is pointable inside finished blades (impregnated, not eaten like coolant), so tools contain it.
si.wafer.diamond.grit.note: Established: synthetic saw-grade grit belt process + abrasive use (same passage as si.wafer.diamond process note). Not established: which maker supplied wafer-slicing blades in 1982.

si.ingot.name: 100mm CZ monocrystalline silicon ingot
si.ingot.description: The 100mm Czochralski monocrystalline boule the wafers are sliced from: boron-doped p-type, 75-150mm diameter per the CZ node, sawn/lapped/polished into si.wafer. Missing link between metal.silica.czochralski (produces nothing) and si.wafer.slicing (consumes nothing).

mb.cpu.fe.contacts.alsi-feed.name: Al-1pctSi evaporation/sputter feed

mb.cpu.fe.contacts.alsi-feed.note: Hedged: exact charge form (wire, slug, sputter target) and 0.5-1% band endpoints beyond the candidate quote not established.

mb.cpu.fe.passivation.teos.name: Tetraethyl orthosilicate PSG precursor

mb.cpu.fe.passivation.teos.note: Hedged: TEOS-vs-silane PSG route split at this fab not established; PECVD nitride alternative explicitly unconfirmed per candidate note and is NOT modeled.

mb.cpu.fe.photoresist.dnq.description: Factory-mixed positive photoresist: diazonaphthoquinone sensitizer in novolac resin, as-spun 1-2 um, developed in dilute TMAH. Consumable distinguished from the chem.photoresist process/family node.

mb.discretes.bjt.resist.name: Planar-BJT DNQ resist formulation
mb.discretes.bjt.resist.description: Positive DNQ/novolac resist formulation consumed by the planar epitaxial BJT mask levels (isolation, base, emitter, contact). Same substance as the CPU resist, scoped here for central merge.

mb.discretes.epi.subcollector.name: n+ subcollector diffusion

mb.discretes.isolation.resist.name: Isolation-mask DNQ resist formulation
mb.discretes.isolation.resist.description: Positive DNQ/novolac resist formulation for the isolation/base/emitter window masks of the planar epitaxial flow. Scoped merge candidate with sibling resist nodes.

mb.discretes.led.epi.junction-die.name: LPE GaP/GaAsP junction die
mb.discretes.led.epi.junction-die.description: Epitaxial double-heterostructure junction die as grown by liquid-phase epitaxy: alternating Zn-doped p-type and S-doped n-type GaP/GaAsP layers a few microns thick, before die attach and epoxy lens packaging.

mb.discretes.led.gallium.recovery.name: Gallium recovery from Bayer liquor
mb.discretes.led.gallium.recovery.description: Alkaline ion-exchange/liquor-treatment recovery of trace gallium from Bayer-process aluminate liquor and bauxite/zinc residues, refined to 99.9-99.99% metal.

mb.discretes.led.substrate.phosphorus.name: Semiconductor-grade white phosphorus feed
mb.discretes.led.substrate.phosphorus.description: High-purity white-phosphorus (P4) feed for GaP substrate growth and GaP/GaAsP LPE charges, via the phosphate-rock electric-furnace route.
mb.discretes.led.substrate.phosphorus.note: Hedged: GaAs-vs-GaP substrate selection per candidate unresolved; arsenic-metal side has no canonical node and stays open.

mb.discretes.test.curve-tracer.name: Discrete curve tracer and bin tester
mb.discretes.test.curve-tracer.description: Semiconductor curve tracer with wafer-probe card plus packaged-part bin tester grading hFE/VCEO (bipolar) and leakage/drop (rectifiers); distinct from the powered C64-board functional station.

mb.vic.process.resist.description: Positive DNQ/novolac resist formulation for the VIC-II mixed digital/analogue silicon-gate flow (9-10 mask levels, single aluminium layer).

si.attach.diced-die.name: Diced known-good die

si.emc.resin.formaldehyde.name: Aqueous formaldehyde feed
